BE = (Z × m_p + N × m_n - M) × c^2 (Unknown)

fields.title: Potential Energy
fields.variables: PE = Potential energy,  m = Mass,  g = Acceleration due to gravity,  h = Height above surface
fields.description: Energy stored in a body due to its position above ground
fields.when_to_use: When calculating stored energy in raised objects, such as water or reservoirs
fields.mnemonic: “Height times weight” — how much energy is stored just by lifting something up.
fields.example: m = 5 kg, g = 9.8 m/s², h = 3 m. Find PE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this assumes CONSTANT g — only a good approximation near a planet's surface, not
for large height changes (use U=−GMm/r instead).
• Forgetting h must be measured from a clearly chosen reference level — PE has no absolute
meaning, only differences matter physically.
• Confusing this with elastic PE (½kx²) — a completely different storage mechanism.

fields.title: Ohm's Law
fields.variables: V = Voltage,  I = Electric current,  R = Resistance
fields.description: Voltage(v) across conductor is directly proportional to the curent flowing through it
fields.when_to_use: When designing and analyzing basic resistive circuits and sizing resistors
fields.mnemonic:
“Voltage is the push, resistance is the pushback, current is what gets through” — three ways to
rearrange one relationship
fields.example: I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω. Find V?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting Ohm's law only applies to “ohmic” components with constant R — diodes and hot
filament bulbs are non-ohmic.
• Confusing V (potential difference across a component) with EMF (total voltage supplied, which
may differ due to internal resistance).
• Mixing up which quantity to isolate when rearranging (R=V/I vs I=V/R).

fields.title: Momentum
fields.variables: p = Linear momentum,  m = Mass,  v = Velocity
fields.description: It is the quantity of motion possessed by a body.A heavier or faster object has greater momentum
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing collisions, explosions, or any process where momentum conservation applies
fields.mnemonic: “Mass in motion” — momentum combines how much mass is moving and how fast.
fields.example: m = 5 kg, v = 4 m/s. Find p?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting momentum is a VECTOR, in the same direction as velocity.
• Confusing momentum with kinetic energy — both involve mass and velocity, but momentum is
linear in v while KE is quadratic.
• Forgetting momentum, not velocity or KE individually, is what's actually conserved in every
collision.

fields.title: Newton's First Law of Motion
fields.variables: ΣF = Net external force acting on the body,  a = Resulting acceleration
fields.description: If the net external force acting on a body at rest is zero, the body will remain at rest.
fields.when_to_use: When establishing the concept of inertia and identifying when a body is in equilibrium
fields.mnemonic:
“No net push, no change in motion” — objects don't need a force to keep moving, only to change
how they move.
fields.example:
A hockey puck on frictionless ice experiences zero net horizontal force, so it continues at constant
velocity indefinitely (a conceptual example — no calculation needed).
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is about NET force — individual forces (gravity, normal force) can act as long as
they cancel.
• The common misconception that motion itself requires a continuously applied force — it's a
CHANGE in motion that requires one.
• Forgetting “constant velocity” includes the special case of remaining at rest.

fields.title: Gravitational Force
fields.variables: F = Gravitational force,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  m1 , m2  = Interacting masses,  r = Separation distance
fields.description: Force of attraction between two masses.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating attractive forces between celestial bodies, satellites, or everyday masses
fields.mnemonic:
“Newton's original inverse-square law” — every pair of masses attracts, weakening with the
square of distance
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing G (a universal constant, always fixed) with g (acceleration due to gravity, which varies
by location).
• Forgetting r is measured between the CENTRES of the two masses, not their surfaces.
• Forgetting this force is always attractive — there's no repulsive gravity in classical mechanics.

fields.title: Escape Velocity
fields.variables: v = Escape velocity,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Mass of celestial body, R = Radius of celestial body
fields.description: Minimum Velocity(v) to escape Earth's gravity(gR)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the launch speed needed for spacecraft to leave a planet's or moon's gravitational field
fields.mnemonic: “√2 times faster than orbital velocity” — escaping needs more speed than merely orbiting.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting escape velocity is independent of the mass of the escaping object itself.
• Forgetting this is the MINIMUM speed needed with no further propulsion — real spacecraft often
use more complex trajectories.
• Confusing this with orbital velocity, which is smaller by a factor of √2.

fields.title: Coulomb's Law
fields.variables: F = Electrostatic force,  k = Coulomb's constant,  q1,q2 = Point charges,  r = Seperation between them
fields.description: Force between two electric charges.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating forces between charged particles in electrostatics and atomic-scale interactions
fields.mnemonic:
“Same shape as gravity, but for charges” — inverse-square law, swap masses for charges and G
for k.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the inverse-SQUARE dependence — doubling distance reduces force to a quarter.
• Forgetting the formula gives magnitude only; direction (attract/repel) must be reasoned
separately from the charge signs.
• Confusing k (Coulomb's constant, 9×109
) with G (gravitational constant) — very different values
despite the similar-looking formula.

fields.title: Electric Charge
fields.variables: Q = Electric charge,  I = Electric current,  t = Time
fields.description: Charge flowing through a Conductor.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating total charge delivered in charging batteries or through a circuit over time
fields.mnemonic:
“Steady current over time adds up to charge” — charge is current multiplied (or integrated) over
time.
fields.example: I = 3 A, t = 10 s. Find Q?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this simple multiplication only works for CONSTANT current — varying current needs
the area under an I-t graph.
• Confusing Q (total charge, coulombs) with I (rate of flow, amperes).
• Forgetting conventional current direction is opposite to actual electron flow in a wire.

fields.title: Electric Power
fields.variables: P = Electric power,  V = Voltage,  I = Current
fields.description: Rate of electrical energy consumption.
fields.when_to_use: When rating electrical appliances, calculating energy bills, or sizing circuit components
fields.mnemonic:
“Voltage times current, the electrical workhorse formula” — the electrical analogue of P=Fv in
mechanics.
fields.example: V = 220 V, I = 5 A. Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is the same underlying relationship as P=I²R=V²/R for purely resistive loads.
• Forgetting AC circuits with a phase difference between V and I need an extra power-factor term:
P=VIcosφ.
• Confusing instantaneous/average power with total energy consumed, which requires multiplying
by time.

fields.title: Time Period of Simple Pendulum
fields.variables: T = Time period,  l = Length of pendulum,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: Time Period depends only on length and gravity for small oscillations.
fields.when_to_use: When designing clocks, measuring local gravitational acceleration, or studying periodic motion
fields.mnemonic: “Longer string, lazier swing” — period depends only on length and gravity, not mass or amplitude.
fields.example: L = 1 m, g = 9.8 m/s². Find T?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting T is independent of the pendulum's mass — worth double-checking in any problem.
• Forgetting this formula is only accurate for SMALL angular amplitudes (roughly under 15°).
• Confusing this with the physical pendulum formula T = 2π√(I/mgd), which uses moment of
inertia instead of just length.

fields.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
fields.variables: ∆x = Uncertainty in position,  ∆p = Uncertainty in momentum,  h = Planck's constant
fields.description: The principle states that the exact positon and momentum of any moving particle cannot be known simultaneously.
fields.when_to_use: When exploring quantum-scale limits of measurement in atomic and subatomic systems
fields.mnemonic:
“You can't pin down both at once” — more precise position means less precise momentum, and
vice versa
fields.example: Δx = 1×10^-10 m. Find the minimum possible Δp?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is a fundamental limit of nature, not a limitation of measuring instruments.
• Treating the inequality as an equality — actual uncertainty can be larger than this minimum,
never smaller.
• Confusing this position-momentum pair with the similar but distinct energy-time uncertainty
relation.

fields.title: Stefan-Boltzmann Law
fields.variables: E = Radiant energy emitted per unit area per unit time,   σ = Stefan-Boltzmann constant,  T = Absolute surface temperature
fields.description: Radiated Energy(E) is proportional to the fourth power of Temperature(T).
fields.when_to_use: When estimating thermal radiation from stars, furnaces, or any heated black-body surface
fields.mnemonic:
“Temperature rules everything” — radiated energy explodes with the fourth power of
temperature.
fields.example:
T = 300 K, σ = 5.67×10^-8 W/(m²K⁴).
 Find E per unit area?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting T must be in Kelvin — essential before raising to the 4th power.
• Forgetting the T⁴ dependence — doubling absolute temperature increases radiated power
16-fold.
• Forgetting this gives power PER UNIT AREA — total power needs multiplying by the object's
surface area.

fields.title: Power
fields.variables: P = Power,  W = Work done,  t = Time required
fields.description: Power(P) describes Rate of doing work(W) in a given time(t).
fields.when_to_use: When rating engines, appliances, or comparing the performance of machines doing work over time
fields.mnemonic:
“How fast work gets done” — the same total work can mean very different power depending on
the time taken.
fields.example: W = 500 J, t = 10 s. Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting power measures the RATE of doing work, not the total work itself.
• Confusing this general definition with context-specific power formulas (P=VI, P=Fv) — all
consistent, just different setups.
• Forgetting energy = power×time is the rearranged form often needed in real problems (like
electricity bills in kWh).

fields.title: Pressure
fields.variables: P = Pressure,  F = Force exerted,  A = Area
fields.description: Pressure(P) is defined as Force(F) applied per area(A).
fields.when_to_use: When calculating fluid pressure, stress on surfaces, or force distribution over an area
fields.mnemonic:
“Same force, smaller area, bigger squeeze” — pressure is force spread (or concentrated) over
area
fields.example: F = 100 N, A = 0.02 m². Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting pressure is a scalar, unlike the force that creates it.
• Confusing pressure with force itself — a small force over a tiny area still creates huge pressure
(like a needle).
• Forgetting 1 Pascal equals exactly 1 N/m².

fields.title: Ideal Gas Equation
fields.variables: P = Pressure,  V = Volume,  n = Number of moles,  R = Universal gas constant,  T = Temperature
fields.description: Relation between pressure(P), volume(V) and temperature(T) of the gas.
fields.units: P (Pa),  V (m^{3}), n (mol),  R (\frac{J \times mol}{K})  T (Kelvin/K)
fields.when_to_use: When performing calculations involving gas behaviour under varying pressure, volume, or temperature conditions
fields.mnemonic:
“Everything a gas does, tied together in one law” — Boyle's, Charles's, and Gay-Lussac's are all
special cases of this.
fields.example: n = 2 mol, T = 300 K, V = 0.05 m³, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting T must be in Kelvin, not Celsius.
• Mixing up R's numeric value across unit systems (8.314 J/mol·K vs 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K).
• Forgetting this assumes an IDEAL gas — real gases deviate, especially at high pressure or low
temperature.

fields.title: Impulse
fields.variables: J = Impulse,  F = Force applied,  ∆t = Time interval of application
fields.description: Change in Momentum due to Force(F) applied.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing collisions, cushioning systems, or impact forces during sudden stops
fields.mnemonic:
“Force held over time equals momentum change” — impulse and Δmomentum are literally the
same thing
fields.example: F = 50 N, Δt = 0.2 s. Find J?
fields.answer: J = 50×0.2 = 10 N·s (10 kg·m/s change in momentum)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting J = Δp always — impulse isn't separate from momentum change, it IS the momentum
change.
• Assuming F must be constant — for a varying force, J is the area under the F–t graph.
• Forgetting impulse is a vector, pointing in the direction of the net applied force.

fields.title: Snell's Law
fields.variables: n1 , n2  = Refractive indices of the first and second media,  θ 1 , θ 2  = Angles of incidence and refraction
fields.description: Describes how light bends when passing from one medium into another.
fields.when_to_use: When designing lenses, optical fibres, or predicting the bending of light through prisms and water
fields.mnemonic:
“Bend toward the slower side” — light bends toward the normal entering a denser (higher n)
medium.
fields.example:
n
1
 =1 (air), θ1
=30°, n2
 =1.5 (glass). Find θ2
?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting angles are measured from the NORMAL, not from the surface itself.
• Forgetting light bends AWAY from the normal entering a less dense medium, toward it entering a
denser one.
• Mixing up which n and θ belong to the incident vs refracted side.

fields.title: Mirror Formula
fields.variables: v = Image distance,  u = Object distance,  f = Focal length of the mirror
fields.description: Relates the focal length(f) of the mirror to object(u) and image distance(v).
fields.when_to_use: When locating images formed by concave or convex mirrors in optics problems and instrument design
fields.mnemonic:
“Mirrors add, lenses subtract” — an easy way to remember the sign difference from the lens
formula.
fields.example: Concave mirror, f = −15 cm, u = −30 cm. Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting mirrors and lenses use DIFFERENT formulas — addition here vs subtraction for lenses.
• Forgetting f is negative for concave mirrors and positive for convex mirrors in the standard
convention.
• Mixing up which distances count as negative, measured against the direction of incident light

fields.title: Electric Potential Energy
fields.variables: U = Electrical potential energy,  k = Couloumb's constant,   q1,q2 = Interacting charges,  r = Distance between those point charges
fields.description: Potential energy(U) stored in a system of two point charges(q1 & q2).
fields.when_to_use: When calculating energy required to assemble or seperate the systems of charged particles
fields.mnemonic:
“Same-sign charges cost energy to bring together, opposite signs release it” — the sign of U tells
you repulsive vs attractive.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting U is positive for like charges (repulsive) and negative for opposite charges
(attractive).
• Confusing this electric potential ENERGY (U, joules, for a pair of charges) with electric potential
(V, volts, at a point).
• Forgetting r is the distance BETWEEN the two charges, not from some external reference.

fields.title: Capacitance
fields.variables: C = Capacitance,  Q = Charge,  V = Voltage
fields.description: Capacitance(C) is the ability of a body to store the electric charge(Q).
fields.when_to_use: When designing charge-storage components for filters, timing circuits
fields.mnemonic: “How much charge for how little voltage” — bigger C stores more charge per volt applied.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting C is a property of the capacitor's geometry (plate area, gap, dielectric), not something
that changes with Q or V — only their ratio stays fixed.
• Confusing capacitance (farads) with charge (coulombs) — very different quantities.
• Assuming larger capacitance means less stored charge — it's the opposite, for a given voltage.

fields.title: Magnetic force on a charge
fields.variables: F = Magnetic force,  q = Magnitude of charge,  v = Speed of charge particle,  B = Magnetic field,  θ = Angle of movement
fields.description: Force(F) on a charged particle(q) moving in a magnetic field(B).
fields.when_to_use: When tracking the circular paths or charged particles in cyclotrons, mass spectrometers
fields.mnemonic: “No motion, no magnetic force” — a stationary charge feels nothing, however strong B is.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this force is always perpendicular to both v and B — it never points along the velocity
direction.
• Forgetting the magnetic force does zero work on the charge, being always perpendicular to
velocity.
• Forgetting motion parallel to B (θ=0°) gives zero force — charges moving along field lines feel
nothing.

fields.title: Torque
fields.variables: τ = Torque,  r = Distance from axis to point of force applied,  F = Force applied,  θ = Angle between force and postion vector
fields.description: Torque is the tendency to rotate an object.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing rotational equilibrium, wrench mechanics or turning of levers
fields.mnemonic:
“Only the perpendicular push counts” — pushing straight along the lever arm produces zero
torque.
fields.example: r = 0.5 m, F = 20 N, θ = 90°. Find τ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting θ is the angle between the position vector r and the force F, not some other angle in
the diagram.
• Forgetting torque is maximum at θ=90° and zero at θ=0° or 180°.
• Forgetting torque has a direction (clockwise/counterclockwise, or via the right-hand rule) — it
isn't just a magnitude.

fields.title: Angular Momentum
fields.variables: L = Angular momentum,  I = Moment of inertia,  ω = Angular velocity,  m = Mass,  v = Linear velocity,  r = Radius
fields.description: Angular Momentum(L) is rotational equivalent of Linear Momentum.
fields.units: L (\frac{kg⋅m^{2}}{s}),  I (kg⋅m^{2}),  ω (\frac{rad}{s}),  m (kg),  v (\frac{m}{s}),  r  (m)
fields.when_to_use: When applying conservation of angular momentum to spinnig skaters, planetary orbits
fields.mnemonic:
“Spin's momentum” — same idea as linear momentum, scaled by how mass is distributed and
how fast it spins.
fields.example: A point mass m = 2 kg moves in a circle of r = 0.5 m at v = 4 m/s. Find L?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting L=Iω is for an extended rotating body, while L=mvr is specifically for a point mass in
circular motion — pick whichever matches the problem.
• Forgetting angular momentum is conserved whenever no external torque acts — a hugely useful
shortcut.
• Confusing L (angular momentum) with l (the quantum number) in atomic physics contexts —
same letter, different meaning.

fields.title: Carnot Efficiency
fields.variables: η = Carnot efficiency,  T_C = Temperature of cold reservoir,  T_H = Temperature of hot reservoir
fields.description: Maximum possible efficiency of a heat engine operating at two different temperatures.
fields.when_to_use: When establishing theoretical performance for engines, refrigerators
fields.mnemonic:
“The bigger the temperature gap, the closer to perfect” — efficiency approaches 1 only as T_C
→0.
fields.example:
T
_H
 = 500 K, T_C 
= 300 K. Find η?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using Celsius instead of Kelvin — this ratio is only meaningful with absolute temperature.
• Forgetting this is the theoretical MAXIMUM efficiency for any engine between these
temperatures — real engines always do worse.
• Forgetting η = 100% only in the impossible limit TC
 = 0 K.

fields.title: Relative Velocity
fields.variables: v_AB = Relative velocity between A&B,  v_A = Velocity of A,  v_B = velocity of B
fields.description: The Velocity of Object A as observed from Object B.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing motion observed from moving frames, such as river-crossing
fields.mnemonic: “How B looks from A's point of view” — subtract the other object's velocity vector from your own.
fields.example:
v
_A
 = (5,0) m/s, v_B
 = (2,3) m/s. Find v_AB?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is a VECTOR subtraction — direction matters, especially in 2D problems.
• Mixing up vAB (A relative to B) with vBA (B relative to A) — they are exact negatives of each
other.
• Forgetting both velocities must be measured in the same reference frame before subtracting.

fields.title: Maximum Height(Projectile)
fields.variables: H = Maximum vertical height,  u = Initial velocity,  θ = Angle of projection,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: Maximum Vertical Height(H) reached by a projectile.
fields.when_to_use: When determining peak altitude of thrown or launched objects in projectile motion
fields.mnemonic:
“Only the vertical launch speed matters for height” — sin²θ extracts just the vertical component's
contribution.
fields.example: u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s². Find H?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the angle term is squared (sin²θ), not just sinθ.
• Confusing maximum height with range, which uses sin(2θ) instead of sin²θ.
• Forgetting this assumes no air resistance and level launch/landing ground.

fields.title: Friction Force
fields.variables: f = Friction force,  μ = Coefficient of friction,  N = Normal force,  m = Mass,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: Friction force(f) resists/opposes the motion of object(N) in opposite direction. The negative sign just displays that N and f are opposite to each other. No need to use negative sign in answer.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating stopping distances, traction requirements
fields.mnemonic: “Grip times the push into the surface” — friction depends on normal force, not contact area.
fields.example: μ = 0.3, m = 5 kg, g = 10 m/s² (flat surface). Find f?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting N is the NORMAL force, which equals mg only on a flat horizontal surface — on an
incline, N = mg cosθ instead.
• Forgetting this gives the MAXIMUM friction available — actual static friction can be anything up
to this value.
• Forgetting friction is independent of the apparent contact area, a genuinely counterintuitive but
true fact.

fields.title: Elastic Potential Energy
fields.variables: PE = Elastic potential energy,  k = Spring constant,  x = Displacement from natural length
fields.description: Energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing energy stored in springs, bungee cords
fields.mnemonic:
“Springs store energy in the square of their stretch” — doubling displacement quadruples stored
energy.
fields.example: k = 150 N/m, x = 0.2 m. Find PE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the ½ factor at the front.
• Forgetting x is displacement FROM the natural (unstretched) length, not the spring's total length.
• Confusing this with gravitational PE (mgh) — a completely different storage mechanism.

fields.title: Time Period of a Satellite
fields.variables: T = Time period,  r = Orbital radius,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Mass of central body
fields.description: Time (T) taken by a Satellite to complete one full orbit.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating how long does a satellite takes to complete one revolution, useful for geostationary satellite placements
fields.given_by: combining Newton's Law of Gravitation with the mechanics of circular motion — this is Kepler's Third Law (T² ∝ r³) made exact, with Newton's gravitational constant and central mass revealing the actual proportionality Kepler could only observe empirically
fields.mnemonic:
“Kepler's third law, written out in full” — same r³∝T² relationship, now with the actual constant
included
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting r is measured from the planet's CENTRE, not from its surface.
• Forgetting G must be paired with M, the mass of the body being orbited, not the satellite's own
 mass.
• Confusing this with Kepler's bare proportionality (T²∝r³), which lacks this formula's actual
 constant.

fields.title: Work done by Gas (Isobaric)
fields.variables: W = Work done,  P = Constant pressure,  ΔV = Change in volume
fields.description: Work done(W) by the gas when Pressure(P) remains constant.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing constant pressure heating or cooling processes such as gas expanding in a piston
fields.given_by: direct consequence of integrating W = ∫P dV under constant pressure — since P doesn't change, the integral reduces to simply P times the volume change
fields.mnemonic:
“Constant pressure pushes through changing volume” — the simplest gas work formula, no
calculus needed.
fields.example: P = 200,000 Pa, ΔV = 0.002 m³. Find W?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this simple form applies ONLY at constant pressure — isothermal or adiabatic
processes need calculus-based work formulas.
• Missing the sign convention: W is positive when the gas expands, negative when compressed.
• Confusing this with the general dW term in the first law, which only takes this specific form for
isobaric processes.

fields.title: Kirchoff's Voltage Law
fields.variables: V = Potential drop or EMF encountered around closed loop
fields.description: Sum of all voltages in a closed loop is always zero.
fields.when_to_use: When solving for unknown currents or voltages in circuits containing multiple loops
fields.mnemonic: “Round trip, net zero” — total voltage change around any closed loop is zero
fields.example: A loop has an EMF of 12 V and two resistive drops of 5 V and 7 V. Check consistency
fields.common_mistakes:
• Losing track of sign conventions (rises vs drops) while traversing the loop in one consistent
direction.
• Applying this to an open (non-closed) path, where it simply doesn't hold.
• Confusing this loop rule with KCL, the node/junction rule.

fields.title: Kirchoff's Current Law
fields.variables: I_in = Currents entering the junction,  I_out = Current leaving the junction
fields.description: Total Current entering a junction equals total current leaving it.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing current distribution at junctions in complex multi-branch circuit networks
fields.mnemonic: “What flows in, must flow out” — charge conservation at a junction.
fields.example:
A junction has incoming currents 3 A and 2 A, and one outgoing branch of 3 A. Find the second
outgoing current?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this applies at a single junction/node, not across an entire circuit.
• Getting the sign/direction of each current wrong when writing the equation.
• Confusing this with KVL, which governs voltage around a loop, not current at a node.

fields.title: Wheatstone Bridge
fields.variables: P,Q,R,S = Resistances of four bridge arms
fields.description: Condition for a balanced Wheatstone  bridge (no current through galvanometer)
fields.when_to_use: When precisely measuring unknown resistance by balancing it against known standard resistors
fields.mnemonic:
“Balance means zero current through the galvanometer” — the condition is a ratio equality, not a
sum.
fields.example: P = 10 Ω, Q = 20 Ω, S = 30 Ω. Find R for balance?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this equality holds only when the bridge is BALANCED — off-balance requires full
circuit analysis instead.
• Mixing up which resistor sits in the numerator vs denominator on each side of the ratio.
• Forgetting the bridge's whole purpose is to find one unknown resistance by comparison with
three known ones.

fields.title: Power Dissipated
fields.variables: P = Power dissipated,  I = Electric current,  R = Resistance,  V = Total voltage
fields.description: Electrical Power converted into heat in a resistor
fields.when_to_use: When calculating heat losses in wire, resistors
fields.given_by: James Prescott Joule through experiments showing that electrical current passing through a resistor generates heat — the rate of heat dissipation is proportional to the square of the current and the resistance
fields.mnemonic: “Three faces of the same fact” — use whichever pair of quantities you're actually given.
fields.example: V = 12 V, R = 4 Ω. Find P?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting these three forms are freely interchangeable only in a purely resistive circuit.
• Picking a form that doesn't match the given data, forcing an unnecessary extra step (e.g.
needing V=IR first).
• Confusing power dissipated as heat in one component with total power delivered by a source in
a multi-element circuit.

fields.title: Force on Current-carrying  Conductor
fields.variables: F = Magnetic Force on conductor,  B = Magnetic field,  I = Electric current,  L = Length of conductor,  θ = Angle between conductor and field
fields.description: Magnetic force experienced by a current-carrying conductor in magnetic field.
fields.when_to_use: When designing electric motors, loudspeakers or any device converting electrical energy in mechanical motion
fields.given_by: Lorentz force law applied to the collective motion of charge carriers in a wire — since current is charge in motion, a magnetic field exerts a net force on the entire conductor, not just individual charges
fields.mnemonic: “Current, field, and length all pitch in — but only the perpendicular part of the angle counts.”
fields.example: B = 0.5 T, I = 3 A, L = 2 m, θ = 90°. Find F?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting θ is the angle between the current direction and B — if they're parallel (θ=0°), the
force is zero.
• Forgetting the direction of F follows the right-hand rule (F = IL×B), perpendicular to both I and B.
• Confusing this with the force on a single moving charge (F = qvB sinθ) — related but distinct
formula.

fields.title: Magnetic Field of Solenoid
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field,   μ₀ = Permeability of free space,  I = Electric current, n = Number of turns
fields.description: Uniform magnetic field inside a long solenoid
fields.when_to_use: When designing electromagnets, inductors or magnetic field source for laboratory experiments
fields.given_by: direct consequence of Ampère's Law — remarkably, the magnetic field inside an ideal solenoid is uniform throughout its interior and zero outside, regardless of the coil's diameter
fields.mnemonic: “Turns per length, times current” — n here means turns PER UNIT LENGTH, not total turns.
fields.example: n = 1000 turns/m, I = 2 A. Find B?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using total turns N instead of turns-per-length n — a very common mix-up.
• Forgetting this formula gives B only deep inside a long (ideal) solenoid, well away from the ends.
• Forgetting the field just outside an ideal solenoid is essentially zero.

fields.title: Energy stored in Inductor
fields.variables: U = Stored magnetic energy,  L = Self-inductance,  I = Current through  inductor
fields.description: Energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor
fields.when_to_use: When designing energy storage in chokes, transformers
fields.given_by: by integrating the power delivered to an inductor (P = Li di/dt) as current rises from zero to I — the magnetic counterpart to energy stored in a capacitor's electric field
fields.mnemonic: “Same shape as kinetic energy, but L replaces m and I replaces v.”
fields.example: L = 2 H, I = 3 A. Find U?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the ½ factor at the front.
• Confusing this stored magnetic energy with a capacitor's stored energy (U = ½CV²) — similar
shape, different circuit element entirely.
• Forgetting this energy returns to the circuit as current decreases — it isn't dissipated like
resistive heating.

fields.title: Photoelectric Effect
fields.variables: KE_max = Maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons,  h = Planck's constant,  f = Frequency of incident light,  ϕ = Work function of metal
fields.description: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons ejected from a metal surface.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing photodetectors, solar cells or threshold behaviour of light-induced electrons
fields.given_by: Albert Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect — proposed that light behaves as discrete energy packets (photons), each capable of ejecting an electron only if its energy exceeds the metal's work function. This work, not relativity, earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics
fields.mnemonic:
“Photon pays the toll” — hf is what's delivered, φ is the toll (work function) to escape, whatever's
left is kinetic energy
fields.example: f = 1×10^15 Hz, φ = 2 eV. Find KEmax?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting KEmax
 is zero (no photoemission at all) whenever hf < φ, no matter how intense the light is.
• Confusing intensity (affects the NUMBER of photoelectrons) with frequency (affects EACH
photon's energy and thus KEmax
) — a very commonly tested distinction.
• Forgetting the work function φ is a material property that differs for every metal.

fields.title: Mass-Energy Equivalence
fields.variables: E = Energy equivalent,  m = Mass,  c = Speed of light
fields.description: A small amount of Mass(m) can generate Large amount of Energy(E)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating energy released in nuclear fission, fusion
fields.mnemonic:
“Mass IS energy, just wearing a costume” — even a tiny mass corresponds to an enormous
energy because c² is so large.
fields.example: m = 1 g = 0.001 kg. Find E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting c must be in m/s (3×108
), not km/s or any other unit, for E to come out in joules.
• Forgetting this gives the maximum theoretical energy locked in a mass — practical processes
(like nuclear reactions) only release 
a small fraction of it.
• Confusing this general relation with the Q-value formula, which computes released energy from
a specific mass DIFFERENCE (Δm), not total mass.

fields.title: Bohr's Energy (nth Orbit)
fields.variables: E_n = Energy of electron in nth orbit,  Z = Atomic number,  n = Principal quantum number
fields.description: Energy of an electron in nth orbit of hydrogen atom.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating spectral lines energies or ionization energies of hydrogen-like atoms
fields.mnemonic:
“Deeper orbit, deeper energy well” — energy becomes more negative (more tightly bound) as n
decreases.
fields.example:
Hydrogen (Z=1), n=2. Find E2
?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the Z² factor for hydrogen-like ions with more than one proton (He+, Li2+) — the
formula reduces to −13.6/n² only for plain hydrogen.
• Forgetting energy is always negative for a bound electron, with n=∞ corresponding to E=0 (a
free electron).
• Confusing the orbit index n with the number of electrons or protons in the atom.

fields.title: Radioactive Decay Law
fields.variables: N = Number of undecayed nuclei at time t,  N_0 = Initial number of nuclei,  λ = Decay constant,  t = Elapsed time
fields.description: Number of radioactive nuclei remaining  after time t.
fields.when_to_use: When modelling carbon dating, nuclear medicine dosing
fields.given_by: Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy while studying thorium decay — established that radioactive substances decay exponentially over time, with the rate of decay proportional to the amount of substance remaining
fields.mnemonic:
“Exponential fade, never quite zero” — the remaining amount decreases smoothly and never
actually reaches zero in finite time.
fields.example: N_0 = 1000 atoms, λ = 0.1/s, t = 10 s. Find N?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting λ and half-life are related by t1/2 = 0.693/λ — easy to mix up which one a problem
 actually gives.
• Forgetting this describes an average/statistical trend over a large number of atoms — for a
small sample, actual decay is random and doesn't trace this smooth curve exactly.
• Forgetting activity A = λN follows the same exponential decay as N itself.

fields.title: Half-Life
fields.variables: t_1/2 = Half-life of a radioactive substance,  λ = Decay constant of a radioactive substance
fields.description: Time required  for half the radioactive nuclei to decay
fields.when_to_use: When estimating the age of radioactive samples or predicting decay timeline of isotopes
fields.given_by: Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy in their early studies of radioactive decay — describes the time required for exactly half of a radioactive sample's nuclei to decay, regardless of the initial quantity
fields.mnemonic:
“0.693 is just ln(2) in disguise” — half-life falls directly out of solving N=N0
/2 in the decay
equation
fields.example: λ = 0.05 per year. Find the half-life?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting 0.693 is just an approximation of ln(2) ≈ 0.6931 — more decimal places give a
 slightly more precise answer.
• Confusing half-life with mean lifetime (τ = 1/λ), which is a different, larger quantity.
• Forgetting half-life is constant for a given isotope, independent of how much substance is
currently present.

fields.title: First Equation of Motion
fields.variables: v = Final velocity,  u = Initial velocity,  a = Uniform acceleration,  t = Time
fields.description: This equation relates the final velocity of an object to its initial velocity, acceleration, and the time for which it has been accelerating.
fields.when_to_use: When solving straight line motion involving constant acceleration
fields.mnemonic:
“The one without displacement” — useful exactly when a problem doesn't mention or ask about
distance.
fields.example: u = 5 m/s, a = 2 m/s², t = 4 s. Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting a is negative for deceleration — sign convention matters relative to the direction of
initial velocity.
• Confusing this with average velocity — this gives the instantaneous final velocity, not an average.
• Assuming u must be zero — it can be any nonzero initial velocity.

fields.title: Range of Projectile (horizontal)
fields.variables: R = Horizontal range,  u = Initial velocity,  θ = Angle of projection,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: The maximum horizontal distance(R) covered by a projectile.
fields.when_to_use: When predicting landing distance of projectile motion problems such as ball games or artillery trajectories
fields.mnemonic: “45 degrees wins” — range is maximized at θ=45°, since sin(2×45°) = sin90° = 1.
fields.example: u = 20 m/s, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s². Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the angle inside the formula is doubled (2θ), not just θ — a very common slip.
• Forgetting this assumes the projectile lands at the same height it launched from — different
launch/landing heights need the full trajectory equations.
• Ignoring that air resistance is neglected here — real projectiles land shorter than this formula
predicts.

fields.title: Centripetal Acceleration
fields.variables: a = Centripetal acceleration,  v = Velocity of a body,  r = Radius of circular path
fields.description: The acceleration(a) of an object moving in a circular path, directed towards the center of the circle.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing object moving in circles, such as vehicle rounding bends or satellites in orbit
fields.mnemonic:
“Tighter turn or faster speed, harder pull toward the centre” — a grows with v squared but only
inversely with r
fields.worked_example: v = 10 m/s, r = 5 m. Find a?
fields.example: v = 10 m/s, r = 5 m. Find a?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this acceleration always points toward the centre of the circular path, never along
 the direction of motion.
• Forgetting a real net force (centripetal force = mv²/r) must supply this acceleration — it doesn't
appear on its own.
• Confusing this with tangential acceleration, which changes speed rather than direction and is
an entirely separate quantity.

fields.title: Work-Energy Theorem
fields.variables: W,ΔKE = Net work done,  m = Mass,  v1,v2 = Initial and final speeds
fields.description: The work done(W) on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.(ΔK.E)
fields.when_to_use: When relating forces acting over a distance to resulting change in an object's speed
fields.given_by: tracing how a force, acting through a displacement, doesn't vanish into nothing but transforms entirely into the energy of motion — bridging the language of forces with the language of speed
fields.mnemonic:
“Net work is exactly the energy gained or lost” — no separate bookkeeping needed once you
know the speeds
fields.example: m = 2 kg, u = 3 m/s, v = 7 m/s. Find the net work done?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting W here is the NET work of ALL forces combined, not just one force acting on the
object.
• Forgetting negative work is common (and expected) whenever a force decelerates the object.
• Confusing this with the rotational analogue, which uses ½Iω² instead of ½mv².

fields.title: Hooke's Law
fields.variables: F = Restoring force,  k = Spring constant,  x = Displacement from equilibrium
fields.description: The force (F) needed to extend or compress a spring by some distance (x) scales linearly with respect to that distance.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing springs, elastic materials
fields.mnemonic: “Springs always push back” — the restoring force always opposes the displacement.
fields.example: k = 200 N/m, x = 0.05 m (stretched). Find F?
fields.answer: F = −200×0.05 = −10 N (a 10 N restoring force, opposing the stretch)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the negative sign, which represents the restoring nature of the force — that's the
whole physical point of the law.
• Assuming k is identical for stretching and compressing — real springs can behave slightly
differently at extremes.
• Forgetting Hooke's law only holds within the elastic limit — beyond that, F is no longer
proportional to x.

fields.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
fields.variables: U = Gravitational potential energy,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M ,m = Interacting masses,  r = Distance between masses
fields.description: The potential energy(U) an object with mass(m) has due to the gravitational potential of its position(r) in a gravitational field(G)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating escape energies, orbital energy budgets or energy changes as object moves within gravitational field
fields.given_by: calculating the work needed to bring a mass from infinity — where gravity's pull is considered zero — into the grip of another body's gravitational field, treating infinite separation as the natural zero point of reference
fields.mnemonic:
“Always negative, always bound” — the minus sign shows the two masses attract, with U rising
(less negative) as they separate.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the negative sign — dropping it reverses the physical meaning entirely.
• Confusing this with the local approximation U = mgh, only valid near a planet's surface for small heights.
• Using weight instead of mass m in the formula.

fields.title: Banking of Roads
fields.variables: θ = Angle of banking,  v = Velocity of vehicle,  r = Radius of curve,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: The practice of raising the outer edge of a curved road surface at a specific angle relative to the horizontal.
fields.when_to_use: When designing highways, racetracks or railway tracks
fields.given_by: tilting the road surface itself so that a component of the normal force supplies the centripetal pull needed for circular motion, easing the burden that friction alone would otherwise have to carry
fields.mnemonic: “Faster turn, steeper tilt” — the ideal banking angle grows with the square of speed.
fields.example: v = 20 m/s, r = 100 m, g = 10 m/s². Find θ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is the ideal banking angle assuming NO friction is needed — real roads combine
banking with friction, allowing a range of safe speeds.
• Using an arbitrary speed instead of the specific design speed the road was banked for.
• Confusing r (radius of the curve) with the road's width or a car's steering radius.

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (Rod)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of rod,  L = Length of rod
fields.description: It is  measure of an object's resistance(I) to changes in its rotational motion, depending on both its mass(M) and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(L)
fields.when_to_use: When modelling rotation of rods, beams
fields.given_by: integrating the mass distributed along a thin rod's length, where each tiny element's contribution to rotational inertia grows with the square of its distance from the rod's midpoint
fields.mnemonic:
“Centre axis keeps I small” — rotating about the middle, mass stays close to the axis on both
sides.
fields.example: M = 1.5 kg, L = 2 m, rotation about the centre. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is specifically for rotation about the CENTRE — rotating about one END instead
uses I = (1/3)ML² (four times larger).
• Confusing L (rod length) with R (used in disk/sphere formulas) — a rod problem has no radius
 here.
• Assuming this applies to a thick or non-uniform rod — it assumes a thin, uniform one.

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (disk)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of disk,  R = Radius of disk
fields.description: The measure of an object's resistance(I) to changes in its rotational motion, depending on both its mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(R)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing rotating wheels, disks or pulleys
fields.given_by: integrating over concentric rings of mass spread across a flat circular disk, each ring resisting rotation in proportion to how far it sits from the axis running through the center
fields.mnemonic:
“A disk splits the difference” — its coefficient (½) sits between a thin rod about its centre (1/12)
and a hoop (1).
fields.example: M = 3 kg, R = 0.2 m. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing a solid disk (½MR²) with a thin ring/hoop (MR², no fraction) — the disk's mass fills the
whole face, the hoop's sits only at the rim.
• Forgetting this is I about the axis through the centre, perpendicular to the disk's face — rotating
about a diameter instead gives ¼MR².
• Using diameter instead of radius R.

fields.title: Moment of Inertia (sphere)
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  M = Mass of sphere,  R = Radius of sphere
fields.description: The  measure of an object's resistance to changes in its rotational motion(I), depending on both its mass(M) and how that mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation(R)
fields.when_to_use: When computing rotational dynamics of spherical bodies such as balls, planets
fields.given_by: integrating the mass of infinitesimally thin disks stacked through a solid sphere, each contributing its own resistance to rotation about the central axis, then summing their effects across the entire volume
fields.mnemonic:
“Mass spread through the whole volume, not just the rim” — a solid sphere's coefficient (2/5) is
smaller than a hollow shell's (2/3).
fields.example: M = 2 kg, R = 0.1 m. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing a solid sphere (2/5 MR²) with a hollow spherical shell (2/3 MR²) — easy to mix up
under pressure.
• Forgetting R is measured from the sphere's centre to its surface.
• Forgetting this formula assumes uniform density throughout the sphere.

fields.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
fields.variables: KE = Rotational kinetic energy,  I = Moment of inertia,  ω = Angular velocity
fields.description: The energy(KE) an object possesses due to its rotation around an axis, determined by its moment of inertia(I) and angular velocity(Ω)
fields.when_to_use: When calculating energy stored in spinning flywheels, rolling objects or rotating machineries
fields.given_by: treating a spinning rigid body as a collection of countless tiny masses, each tracing its own circle at its own speed, and summing up the kinetic energy each carries — but expressed through the single, elegant language of angular velocity
fields.mnemonic: “Same shape as linear KE, but I replaces m and ω replaces v.”
fields.worked_example:
• Forgetting I
c
 must specifically be about an axis through the centre of mass — this theorem
doesn't connect two arbitrary parallel axes.
• Forgetting d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
• Forgetting I about any shifted axis is always ≥ I
c
, never smaller.
fields.example: I = 4 kg·m², ω = 3 rad/s. Find KE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting ω must be in rad/s, not rpm or Hz, before plugging in.
• Forgetting a rolling object has BOTH translational and rotational KE: total = ½mv² + ½Iω².
• Using linear velocity v in place of ω by mistake.

fields.title: Parallel Axis Theorem
fields.variables: I = Moment of inertia,  I_c = Moment of inertia about center of mass,  M = Mass,  d = Perpendicular distance
fields.description: The parallel axis theorem allows calculation of a body's moment of inertia about any axis parallel to one through its center of mass by adding the product of its mass and the square of the distance.
fields.when_to_use: When axis of rotation does not pass through object's center, such as pendulum swinging from a pivot at its edge
fields.mnemonic: “Centre of mass first, then pay a penalty for moving the axis” — you always add, never subtract.
fields.example:
A rod has I_c= (1/12)ML² about its centre.
 Find I about one end (d = L/2)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting I_c must specifically be about an axis through the centre of mass — this theorem
doesn't connect two arbitrary parallel axes.
• Forgetting d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
• Forgetting I about any shifted axis is always ≥ I_c, never smaller.

fields.title: Angular Impulse
fields.variables: J = Angular impulse,  τ = Applied torque,  Δt = Time interval, ΔL = Chnage in angular momentum
fields.description: It quantifies the effect of torque(τ) over a period of  time(t)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing sudden rotational impact, such as cue striking or billiard ball
fields.given_by: extending the idea of linear impulse into rotational motion — considering how a torque, sustained over an interval of time, doesn't just act in an instant but accumulates to change how fast something spins
fields.mnemonic:
“Torque held over time changes spin” — the rotational twin of the linear impulse-momentum
theorem.
fields.example: τ = 5 N·m applied for Δt = 2 s. Find ΔL?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing this rotational impulse with ordinary linear impulse (J = FΔt = Δp) — same structure,
different quantities.
• Forgetting τ must be constant (or an average value) over the interval for this simple form to
apply directly.
• Forgetting angular momentum L, like linear momentum, is a vector — direction matters.

fields.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
fields.variables: dU = Change in internal energy of a system,  dQ = Total heat supplied,  dW = Total work done by the system
fields.description: The Change in Internal Energy(U) of a system is difference of Heat supplied(Q) and Work done(W) by the system.
fields.when_to_use: When tracking energy balance in engines, refrigeration processes
fields.mnemonic:
“What you gain, minus what you spend, stays inside” — internal energy change equals heat
added minus work done BY the system.
fields.example: A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. Find dU?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Mixing up sign conventions — some textbooks define dW as work done ON the system (dU = dQ
+ dW instead), so always check which convention is in use.
• Forgetting Q and W are path-dependent (they depend on the specific process), while U itself is
 a state function.
• Assuming dU = 0 automatically unless the problem explicitly states an isothermal ideal-gas
process.

fields.title: Boyle's Law
fields.variables: P1,P2 = Initial and final pressures,  V1,V2 = Initial and final volumes
fields.description: Describes the relationship between the pressure(P) and volume(V) of a gas at constant temperature.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing isothermal compression or expansion of gas, such as in springes or diving cyclinders
fields.mnemonic:
“Squeeze the volume, pressure pushes back harder” — an inverse relationship at constant
temperature.
fields.example:
P
1
 = 100 kPa, V1
 = 4 L. Find P2
 when V2
 = 2 L.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this only holds at constant temperature — heating or cooling during compression
breaks the relationship.
• Treating P and V as directly proportional instead of inversely proportional.
• Mixing this up with Charles's law, which relates V and T rather than P and V.

fields.title: Charle's Law
fields.variables: V1,V2 = Initial volumes,  T1,T2 = Initial temperature
fields.description: Explains how gases expand or contract upon heating
fields.when_to_use: When scaling thermal expansion boundaries for hot-air baloons, gas cylinders
fields.mnemonic:
“Volume and temperature rise together” — at constant pressure, gas expands proportionally with
absolute temperature.
fields.example:
V1
= 2 L at T1
 = 300 K. Find V2
 at T2
 = 450 K.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using Celsius instead of Kelvin — this ratio only holds with absolute temperature.
• Forgetting this assumes constant pressure — if pressure also changes, the combined gas law is
 needed instead.
• Confusing this with Gay-Lussac's law (P/T = constant at fixed volume), which tracks pressure
instead of volume.

fields.title: Mean Free Path
fields.variables: λ = Mean free path,  n = Number density,  d = Diameter of gas molecule
fields.description: The average distance a particle travels between collisions in a gas, and it is influenced by factors such as particle density and size.
fields.when_to_use: When configuring vaccum chambers, tracing microscopic diffusion barriers
fields.mnemonic: “Bigger molecules, more crowding, shorter free path” — λ shrinks as either n or d grows.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the √2 factor, which accounts for the fact that all molecules are moving, not just the
one you're tracking.
• Confusing number density n (molecules per m³) with moles or mass density.
• Using molecular radius instead of molecular diameter d.

fields.title: Specific Heat Capacity
fields.variables: Q = Transferred heat energy,  m = Mass of substance,  c = Specific heat capacity,  T = Temperature
fields.description: Amount of heat(Q) required to raise the temperature(T) of a unit mass of a substance by one degree Celsius or one Kelvin.
fields.when_to_use: When managing phase boundaries, cooling calculations or balancing industrial caloric exchangers
fields.given_by: the total thermal energy required to change the temperature of a distinct mass of a substance
fields.mnemonic: “More mass, bigger temperature swing, more heat needed” — a simple triple product.
fields.example: m = 2 kg water, c = 4200 J/(kg·K), ΔT = 20 K. Find Q?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Reusing water's c value for a different material — c is specific to each substance.
• Forgetting ΔT is a temperature CHANGE, not an absolute temperature.
• Applying this formula across a phase change (melting/boiling) — that needs latent heat instead,
since temperature stays constant during the phase change.

fields.title: Newton's Law of Cooling
fields.variables: dT/dt = Rate of temperature drop over time,  k = Thermal cooling proportionality constant,  T = Instantaneous body temperature,  T_0 = Surrounding environment temperature
fields.description: The rate at which an object loses heat is proportional to the difference between its temperature(T) and the ambient temperature(T_0)
fields.when_to_use: To model atmospheric temperature decay curves or engineer passive safe cooldown timers for hot mechanical processes
fields.mnemonic:
“Hotter than the room, faster it cools” — the rate of cooling is proportional to how far above the
surroundings the object is.
fields.example:
T
_0
 = 25°C (room), k = 0.05 /min, current T = 80°C. Find the instantaneous cooling rate?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is only a good approximation for small temperature differences — it isn't exact
at every ΔT.
• Missing that the negative sign just means T moves toward T_0, whichever direction that is(cooling if T>T_0, warming if T<T_0).
• Confusing this instantaneous-rate equation with its solved form T(t) = T_0+(Ti−T0)e-kt, which
requires integrating it.

fields.title: Capacitors in Series
fields.variables: 1/C = Total capacitance,  1/C1, 1,C2 = Individual capacitances
fields.description: When capacitors are connected in series, the total capacitance is less than the smallest individual capacitor, and all capacitors carry the same charge while the voltage divides among them.
fields.when_to_use: When distributing a high operating voltage evenly across lower-rated storage components to safeguard circuitry fields
fields.given_by: the fact that capacitors in series carry the same charge, while the total voltage splits across each — the reciprocals of capacitance add, similar in form to resistors in parallel
fields.mnemonic:
“Series capacitors always end up weaker than the weakest one” — like parallel resistors, but for
capacitance
fields.example:
C1
= 2 μF, C2
= 3 μF. Find C?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end to recover C, not 1/C.
• Forgetting series capacitance is always smaller than the smallest individual capacitor — a good
 sanity check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel capacitor formula, which simply adds values directly.

fields.title: Capacitors in Parallel
fields.variables: C = Total capacitance,  C1,C2,C3 = Individual capacitances
fields.description: If all capacitors are connected in parallel then there sum gives us the total capacitance(
fields.when_to_use: To maximize overall static charge accumulation capacities
fields.given_by: the fact that capacitors in parallel share the same voltage, while total charge is the sum of each — so their capacitances simply add, similar in form to resistors in series
fields.mnemonic:
“Parallel capacitors just add their plate area effectively” — straightforward addition, more
capacitance
fields.example:
C1
 = 2 μF,  C2
= 3 μF,  C3
= 5 μF. Find C?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting parallel capacitors add directly — the opposite behaviour of parallel resistors, which
need reciprocals.
• Mixing this up with the series capacitor formula, which requires reciprocals instead.
• Forgetting all parallel capacitors share the same voltage, while charge divides according to
each capacitor's value.

fields.title: Gauss's law
fields.variables: ϕ = Total electric flux,  Q_enc = Total charge enclosed,  ε₀ =   Pemittivity of free space
fields.description: The total electric flux(ϕ) through a closed surface(A) is proportional to the net electric charge(Q) enclosed by that surface.
fields.when_to_use: When deriving field equations for symmetric volumetric objects like charged sphere, coaxial wires
fields.mnemonic:
“Only what's trapped inside the surface counts” — charges outside contribute nothing to the net
flux.
fields.example:
Q_enc
= 4×10-6 C. Find Φ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting Q_enc
 is only the charge inside the Gaussian surface, no matter how close outside
 charges are.
• Choosing a Gaussian surface that doesn't match the symmetry of the charge distribution,
making E hard to isolate from the flux integral.
• Confusing electric flux Φ (field lines through a surface) with the electric field E itself.

fields.title: Electric Field (infinite sheet)
fields.variables: E = Electrical field,  σ = Surface charge density per unit area,  ε₀ = Permittivity of free space
fields.description: The electric field is always perpendicular to the surface of the sheet, pointing away from the sheet if the charge is positive and toward the sheet if negative
fields.when_to_use: When tracking field baselines adjacent to massive capacitor plates
fields.mnemonic:
“An infinite sheet's field doesn't care how far you stand” — E stays constant with distance, unlike
a point charge's field.
fields.worked_example:
• Forgetting series resistance is always greater than any individual resistor — a good sanity
check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel formula, which requires reciprocals.
• Forgetting current is the same through every series resistor, while voltage divides across them
fields.example: σ = 2×10^-6 C/m². Find E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting E is independent of distance from an infinite sheet — a common conceptual trap
since most field formulas do fall off with distance.
• Forgetting the factor of 2, which comes from the field spreading equally to both sides of the
 sheet.
• Confusing σ (surface charge density, C/m²) with a point charge Q (in Coulombs) — different
 quantities entirely.

fields.title: Resistors in Series
fields.variables: R = Total resistance,  R1,R2,R3 = Individual resistances
fields.description: The Total resistance(R) of a substance in series is the sum of all resistors connected in series
fields.when_to_use: When managing current division across multi-component strings
fields.mnemonic: “Series resistors just queue up and add” — no reciprocals needed, unlike parallel.
fields.example:
R1
= 4 Ω, R2
 = 6 Ω, R3
 = 2 Ω. Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting series resistance is always greater than any individual resistor — a good sanity
check.
• Mixing this up with the parallel formula, which requires reciprocals.
• Forgetting current is the same through every series resistor, while voltage divides across them

fields.title: Resistance in Parallel
fields.variables: R = Total network resistance,  R1,R2 = Individual resistances
fields.description: The Total resistance in parallel circuit is the sum of fraction of all resistors.
fields.when_to_use: When building households circuitry grids where components requires independent power loops but equal voltage
fields.mnemonic:
“Parallel resistors always end up weaker together” — total resistance is smaller than even the
smallest individual resistor.
fields.example:
R1
= 6 Ω, R2
= 3 Ω. Find R?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end — the formula directly gives 1/R, not R.
• Forgetting parallel resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistor — a useful
 sanity check.
• Confusing this with the series formula, which simply adds resistances with no reciprocals at all.

fields.title: Joule's Law of Heating
fields.variables: H = Thermal heat energy,  I = Electric current,  R = Electric resistance,  t = Time
fields.description: The heat(H) produced in a conductor by an electric current(I) directly proportional to the square of the current (I²), the resistance (R) of the conductor, and the time (t) for which the current flows
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing electrical heating applications, calculating power transmission losses
fields.mnemonic: “Current squared, not just current” — doubling current quadruples the heat, not just doubles it.
fields.example: I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω, t = 60 s. Find H?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the I² dependence — the single most common slip, treating heat as scaling with I
rather than I².
• Confusing total heat H (joules) with power 
(watts = H/t).
• Applying this to an ideal inductor or capacitor — it only applies to genuinely resistive heating.

fields.title: Biot-Savart Law
fields.variables: dB = Magnetic field vector,  μ₀ = Permeability of free space,  I = Current, dL = Length,  θ = Angle between length vector and position vector,  r = Distance
fields.description: The magnetic field(B) generated by a steady electric current(I), relating it to the current’s magnitude, direction(θ), and geometry(L,r)
fields.when_to_use: To calculate total magnetic field at any point in space near an arbitrarily shaped current-carrying wire
fields.mnemonic:
“Every tiny piece of wire casts its own little magnetic shadow” — you sum contributions from
each current element.
fields.example:
A wire element dl = 0.01 m carries I = 5 A, at perpendicular distance r = 0.1 m (dl ⊥ r̂, so
 sinθ=1). Find dB?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the cross product means only the component of dl perpendicular to r̂ contributes — a
parallel element contributes nothing.
• Forgetting this gives only one tiny element's contribution — finding the total B requires
integrating over the whole current path.
• Confusing this fundamental law with Ampere's law, which is only a shortcut usable in highly
symmetric setups.

fields.title: Ampere's Law
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field,  r = Radius,  μ₀ = Permeability of free space,  I = Electric current
fields.description: Ampère's law relates the magnetic field(B) around a closed loop(2πr) to the electric current(I) passing through that loop.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the magnetic field produced by highly symmetrical current distributions
fields.mnemonic: “Add up B around a loop, get the current locked inside.”
fields.example:
A long straight wire carries I_enc = 10 A. 
Find B at r = 0.05 m.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting I_enc  only counts current actually enclosed by the chosen Amperian loop, ignoring
everything outside it.
• Picking a loop that doesn't match the symmetry of the field, which makes the field impossible
to pull out cleanly from the integral.
• Forgetting this basic form assumes steady (DC) currents — changing electric fields require the
Maxwell correction term.

fields.title: Magnetic Moment
fields.variables: M = Magnetic moment,  n = Number of turns,  I = Current,  A = Area of the loop
fields.description: The magnetic moment(M) is a vector quantity that characterizes the strength and orientation of a magnet.
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the torque exerted on a coil inside an external magnetic field
fields.given_by: Rooted in André-Marie Ampère's insight that a current-carrying loop behaves like a tiny magnet — magnetic moment quantifies the "strength" of this equivalent magnetic dipole, scaling with current, loop area, and number of turns
fields.mnemonic: “Turns times current times area” — three simple ingredients multiplied together.
fields.example: N = 200 turns, I = 0.5 A, A = 0.002 m². Find M?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting A is the loop's cross-sectional area, not its perimeter or side length.
• Forgetting to include N for a coil of multiple turns, not just a single loop.
• Treating this as a plain number when magnetic moment is actually a vector, directed along the
loop's normal via the right-hand rule.

fields.title: Cyclotron Frequency
fields.variables: f  = Cyclotron frequency,  q = Electric charge,  B = Magnetic field strength,  m = Particle mass
fields.description: The natural frequency(f) at which a charged particle orbits in a magnetic field perpendicular to its motion, determined solely by the particle’s charge-to-mass ratio and the magnetic field strength(B)
fields.when_to_use: When designing particle accelerators like cyclotrons or analyzing mass spectrometers
fields.mnemonic: “Heavier charge, slower spin” — frequency depends only on mass and charge, not speed.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this frequency is independent of the particle's speed or the radius of its circular path
— a genuinely surprising and often-tested feature.
• Swapping mass and charge in the formula.
• Confusing this single-particle circular-motion frequency with a full cyclotron accelerator's
output beam energy

fields.title: Lorentz Force
fields.variables: F = Total Lorentz force,  q = Electric charge,  E = Electric field,  v = Particle velocity ,  B = Magnetic field
fields.description: The total force(F) experienced by a charged particle(q) moving through electric field(E) and magnetic fields(B)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing trajectories of electrons or ions in combined electromagnetic environments
fields.mnemonic:
“Electric force pushes straight, magnetic force pushes sideways” — the E-term acts along E, the
magnetic term acts perpendicular to both v and B.
fields.example:
q = 2C, E = 5 N/C (along x), v = 3 m/s (along x),
 B = 2T (along y). Find F?
fields.answer: Electric part: qE = 10 N along x. Magnetic part: v×B has magnitude vB = 6 (along z), so qvB = 12 N along z. Total F = (10, 0, 12) N
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the magnetic term is a cross product — its direction follows the right-hand rule, not
simple magnitude multiplication.
• Forgetting the magnetic force does zero work on the charge (always perpendicular to velocity),
while the electric force can do work.
• Adding E and v×B as if they were simple scalars when they point in different directions — they
must be combined as vectors.

fields.title: Faraday's Law
fields.variables: EMF = Total potential,  N = Coil turns,  dϕ/dt = Change in magnetic flux over time t,  B = Magnetic field,  A = Cross-sectional area
fields.description: It explains how the magnetic field interacts with the electric circuit to produce an EMF
fields.units: EMF (V),  N (counts),  ϕ (Weber/W),  t (s),  B (Tesla),  A (m^{2})
fields.when_to_use: To model rational generator outputs, modern dynamic microphone capture mechanics
fields.mnemonic:
“Changing flux writes voltage” — no change in flux means no EMF, no matter how strong the field
is.
fields.example: Flux through a single loop changes from 0.02 Wb to 0.08 Wb in 0.5 s. Find EMF?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting EMF depends on the RATE of change of flux, not the flux's absolute size — a huge
but constant flux induces nothing.
• Forgetting to multiply by N (number of turns) for a coil: EMF = −N dΦ/dt.
• Dropping the negative sign, which encodes the direction of the induced current via Lenz's law

fields.title: Self Inductance
fields.variables: EMF = Induced potential,  L = Self inductance,  dI/dt = Current shift over time t
fields.description: The property of a coil or circuit that opposes changes in its own current by inducing an electromotive force (EMF) in itself.
fields.when_to_use: When constructing localised signal isolation layers, contactless power charges
fields.mnemonic:
“A coil fights its own current changes” — self-induced EMF always opposes what's happening to
its own current.
fields.example: L = 2 H, dI/dt = 3 A/s. Find EMF?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the negative sign (Lenz's law) — it's not optional, it tells you the direction of
opposition.
• Confusing L (a property of one coil) with M (mutual inductance between two coils).
• Forgetting L depends on the coil's own geometry (turns, area, core material), not on the current
flowing through it.

fields.title: Mutual Inductance
fields.variables: EMF_2 = Induced output emf on second coil,  M = Mutual inductance,  dI/dt = Changing primary current over time t
fields.description: The property of two nearby coils where a changing current in one coil induces an electromotive force (emf) in the other.
fields.when_to_use: When constructing localised signal isolation layers, contactless power charges
fields.mnemonic:
“One coil's changing current writes an EMF into its neighbour” — the minus sign reflects Lenz's
law.
fields.example:
M = 0.5 H, dI1
/dt = 4 A/s. Find EMF_2?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the negative sign, which encodes Lenz's law (the induced EMF opposes the change
causing it).
• Confusing mutual inductance M (between two coils) with self-inductance L (within a single coil).
• Forgetting M depends on the geometry and coupling of both coils together, not just one coil
 alone.

fields.title: Transformer Ratio
fields.variables: V_s/V_p = Secondary and primary voltages,  N_s/N_p = Secondary and primary coils turns,  I_p/I_s = Primary and secondary currents
fields.description: The transformer ratio defines the relationship between the primary and secondary windings, determining how voltage(V) and current (I)are transformed.
fields.when_to_use: When engineering industrial electrical power grids, charging adapters
fields.mnemonic: “More turns, more voltage, less current” — voltage scales with turns, current scales inversely.
fields.example:
N
_p
 = 100 turns, N_s
 = 500 turns, V_p
 = 20 V. 
Find V_s?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the current ratio is inverse to the voltage/turns ratio, not in the same direction.
• Assuming this ideal-transformer relation holds exactly for a real transformer, which always has
some power loss.
• Mixing up subscripts p (primary) and s (secondary).

fields.title: Archimedes' Principle
fields.variables: F_b = Buoyant force,  ρ = Fluid density,  V = Volume,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: Archimedes' principle states that a body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
fields.when_to_use: When verifying aquatic vessel displacements, balloon liftoff thresholds
fields.mnemonic: “You feel lighter by exactly the weight of fluid you displaced.”
fields.example: ρ(water) = 1000 kg/m³, V = 0.002 m³ (displaced volume), g = 9.8.  Find F_b?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting V is the volume of fluid displaced, not the total volume of the object — crucial when
the object floats and is only partly submerged.
• Using the object's own density instead of the fluid's density ρ.
• Forgetting this only gives the buoyant force — whether the object floats or sinks also depends
on comparing F_b to its actual weight.

fields.title: Stokes' Law
fields.variables: F = Total internal force,  η = Viscosity,  r = Radius,  v = Velocity
fields.description: The drag force(F) experienced by small spherical particles moving through a viscous fluid.
fields.when_to_use: When tracking drop mechanics in oil emulsions,  also defines behaviour of rain drops
fields.mnemonic:
“Drag grows in a straight line with size and speed” — unlike air drag at high speed, 
this is linear
 in both r and v
fields.example:
η = 0.001 Pa·s (water), r = 0.005 m, v = 0.02 m/s. 
Find F?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting Stokes' law only holds for small spheres moving slowly through a viscous fluid (low
Reynolds number).
• Confusing this linear-in-v drag with the quadratic-in-v drag formula used at higher speeds or in
turbulent regimes.
• Mixing up η (a fluid property) with r (a property of the sphere).

fields.title: Terminal Velocity
fields.variables: v_t = Terminal velocity,  r = Radius,  ρ = Density of medium,  σ = Surrounding density,  g = Acceleration due to gravity,  η = Viscosity
fields.description: This formula indicates that terminal velocity is reached when the force of gravity is balanced by the drag force acting on the object
fields.when_to_use: When evaluating sediment settling velocities, industrial fluid seperation
fields.mnemonic: “Bigger ball, faster fall” — terminal velocity scales with the square of the radius.
fields.example: r = 0.001 m, ρ = 8000 kg/m³ (steel), σ = 1.2 kg/m³ (air), g = 9.8, η = 1.8×10^-5 Pa·s. Find v_t?
fields.answer: v_t  = \frac{2(0.001)^{2}(7998.8)(9.8)}{(9×1.8×10^{-5})} ≈ 968 m/s (illustrative — assumes Stokes' law still applies)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this formula assumes Stokes' law (viscous drag only, low Reynolds number) — it
breaks down once the flow around the sphere becomes turbulent.
• Forgetting (ρ−σ) is sphere density minus fluid density — if the sphere is less dense than the
fluid, vt
 comes out negative, meaning it rises instead of sinks.
• Confusing η (fluid viscosity) with ρ or σ (densities).

fields.title: Poiseuille's Equation
fields.variables: Q = Volumetric flow,  r = Internal radius,  ΔP = Pressure drop,  η = Viscosity,  L = Tube length
fields.description: This formula  depicts the pressure drop of an incompressible, Newtonian fluid flowing through a long cylindrical pipe under laminar flow conditions.
fields.when_to_use: To compute human hemodynamic blood flow boundaries, microfuild industrial pumps
fields.mnemonic:
“Radius rules everything” — flow rate depends on r to the fourth power, so a small radius change
has a huge effect.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the r⁴ dependence — doubling the radius increases flow rate 16-fold, not just 2 or 4
 times.
• Confusing viscosity η with fluid density ρ — they play very different roles.
• Applying this to turbulent flow or a non-Newtonian fluid, where it no longer holds — it assumes
steady laminar flow.

fields.title: Surface Tension (excess pressure)
fields.variables: ΔP = Net internal excess pressure,  T = Surface tension,  r = Radius
fields.description: It is a property of liquid to shrink due to resistance to external pressure forming drops and bubbles
fields.when_to_use: To calculate structural mechanics for aerosal spray systems or micro droplet formations
fields.given_by: the imbalance of cohesive molecular forces at a liquid's surface, where molecules — pulled inward by their neighbors but with none above to balance them — draw together like an invisible elastic skin stretched taut over the liquid
fields.mnemonic: “A bubble has two surfaces, so it doubles the drop's formula.”
fields.example: Soap bubble: T = 0.03 N/m, r = 0.01 m. Find ΔP?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting a soap bubble has two liquid surfaces (inner and outer film), while a droplet has only
one — that's the entire reason for the factor-of-2 difference.
• Using the drop formula for a bubble or vice versa.
• Using diameter instead of radius r.

fields.title: Capillary Rise
fields.variables: h = Vertical capillary lift/rise,  T = Surface tension,  θ = Angle of contact,  r  = Radius,  ρ = Fluid density,  g = Acceleration due to gravity
fields.description: The phenomenon where a liquid rises or falls in a narrow tube or porous material due to the combined effect of adhesive forces  and cohesive forces.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing botanical soil hydration tracts, microfluid transport diagnostics
fields.given_by: balancing the vertical component of the surface tension force acting along the liquid-glass contact line against the weight of the liquid column raised inside the narrow tube
fields.mnemonic: “The thinnest tube climbs the highest” — smaller radius means greater capillary rise.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting cosθ — for a liquid that doesn't wet the tube well (θ > 90°), cosθ is negative and the
liquid is depressed, not raised.
• Using diameter instead of radius r in the denominator.
• Mixing units (e.g. r in mm while ρ, g are in SI) before combining them.

fields.title: Displacement in SHM
fields.variables: x = Instantaneous displacement,  A = Amplitude,  ω = Angular frequency,  t = Time
fields.description: Displacement in SHM(x) is a sinusoidal function(sin) describing how far an object is from equilibrium at any time, governed by amplitude(A), angular frequency(ω), and phase.
fields.when_to_use: When analysing baseline sinusoidal behaviors across mechanical spring pendulum
fields.given_by: the projection of uniform circular motion onto a straight diameter line, representing the linear position of an oscillating object from equilibrium over time  This explains the foundational geometric mechanism behind how the sinusoidal displacement equation is physically derived
fields.mnemonic:
“Starts at the extreme” — the cosine form assumes the object begins at maximum displacement
(x=A) at t=0.
fields.example: A = 0.1 m, ω = 5 rad/s, t = 0.2 s. Find x?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing the cosine form (starts at the extreme) with the sine form x=Asin(ωt) (starts at the
