centre) — the right choice depends on the initial condition given.
• Forgetting ωt must be evaluated in radians, not degrees.
• Forgetting a general starting condition needs a phase constant: x = Acos(ωt+φ).

fields.title: Energy in SHM
fields.variables: E = Total mechanical energy,  m = Mass,  ω = Angular frequency,  A = Amplitude of oscillation
fields.description: The total mechanical energy  E  of a particle in SHM is the sum of its kinetic energy (KE) and potential energy (PE) and remains constant for an ideal system
fields.when_to_use: When determining energy transitions or peak velocities in ideal vibrating spring-mass systems
fields.given_by: combining Hooke's Law with the kinetic and potential energy expressions for a spring-mass system — shows that total mechanical energy remains constant throughout the oscillation, continuously exchanging between kinetic and potential forms
fields.mnemonic:
“Total energy is locked into amplitude squared” — constant throughout the motion, unlike KE or
PE alone.
fields.example: m = 0.2 kg, ω = 10 rad/s, A = 0.05 m. Find E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is the TOTAL energy (KE+PE), constant at every instant — not the same as
instantaneous KE or PE, which vary with position.
• Using ordinary frequency f instead of angular frequency ω = 2πf directly in the formula.
• Using instantaneous displacement x instead of amplitude A — total energy always uses A.

fields.title: Standing Wave (string)
fields.variables: fn  = Frequency of the n-th harmonic,  n = Harmonic number,  v = Wave speed along the string,  L = Length of string
fields.description: A standing wave on a string is formed when two waves of the same frequency and amplitude travel in opposite directions, creating fixed points called nodes.
fields.when_to_use: When studying musical acoustic profiles of stringed instruments like guitars or violins
fields.given_by: Rooted in Marin Mersenne's 17th-century laws of vibrating strings — one of the earliest quantitative studies in acoustics, showing how a string's pitch depends on its length, tension, and mass per unit length, later explained through wave superposition
fields.mnemonic: “A string behaves like an open pipe for waves” — same 2L rule, and every harmonic is allowed.
fields.example:
L = 1 m, wave speed on the string v = 200 m/s. 
Find the 3rd harmonic?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting v here is the wave speed on the string itself (v = √(T/μ)), not the speed of sound in
 air.
• Confusing this all-harmonics formula with the closed-pipe odd-harmonics-only formula.
• Forgetting this exact form assumes both ends are fixed (or both free) — mixed boundary
conditions change the allowed harmonics.

fields.title: Speed of sound in medium
fields.variables: v = Speed of sound,   B = Bulk modulus of elasticity,   ρ = Density of the medium
fields.description: The speed of sound(v) in a medium is determined by the square root of the ratio of its bulk modulus(B) to its density(ρ)
fields.when_to_use: When computing sound propagation timelines across different liquids, gases, or solid structural components
fields.mnemonic: “Stiffer medium, faster sound; denser medium, slower sound.”
fields.example:
Water: B ≈ 2.2×10^9
Pa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting B (bulk modulus) is different for every material — solids use different elastic moduli
in the analogous formula.
• Confusing this general formula with the ideal-gas-specific version v = √(γRT/M).
• Not realizing v still depends on temperature in gases, even though T doesn't appear explicitly
 here — B itself changes with T.

fields.title: Doppler Effect
fields.variables: f' = Observed frequency,   f = Emitted source frequency,   v = Speed of waves in the medium,  v_o = Velocity of observer,  v_s  = Velocity of source
fields.description: The apparent change in frequency(f ′) observed by the observer w.r.t to the sources'  frequency(f)
fields.when_to_use: When tracking radar speed traps, astrophysical redshift/blueshift observations, or passing emergency sirens
fields.mnemonic:
“Add for an approaching observer, subtract for an approaching source” — the sign flips
depending on who's moving toward whom.
fields.example:
f = 500 Hz, v = 340 m/s (sound speed), 
v_0 = 0(observer at rest), v_s = 20 m/s (source
approaching). Find f'?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Getting the sign wrong for approaching vs receding source or observer — by far the most
common Doppler mistake.
• Applying the same sign rule to v_0 and v_s
 — they sit on opposite sides of the fraction and follow
different logic.
• Using this classical (sound) formula for light — the relativistic Doppler effect has a different  form entirely.

fields.title: Beats Frequency
fields.variables: f_beat  = Beat frequency,  f1 , f2  = Interacting wave frequencies
fields.description: A Beat is interference pattern created by two slightly different frequency waves(f1, f2)
fields.when_to_use: When tuning musical instruments or analyzing close-frequency sound signatures
fields.given_by: Derived from adding two sinusoidal waves of slightly different frequencies — the resulting envelope oscillates at a rate equal to the difference between the two original frequencies, which musicians have long used to tune instruments by ear
fields.mnemonic: “Beats are the tug-of-war difference” between two close frequencies sounding together.
fields.example:
f
1
= 256 Hz, f2
 = 260 Hz. Find the beat frequency?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting beats are only clearly noticeable when f1
 and f2
 are close in value.
• Adding the frequencies instead of subtracting them.
• Forgetting the result is always positive — it's an absolute difference, regardless of which
 frequency is higher.

fields.title: Resonance in Open Pipe
fields.variables: f = Frequency of n-th harmonic,   n = Principal integer,  v = Speed of sound,   L = Length of the pipe
fields.description: Resonance in open pipes occurs when standing waves form, allowing specific frequencies to be amplified, which is essential in musical instruments like flutes and organ pipes.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing wind instruments such as flutes or organ pipes
fields.given_by: Rooted Bernoulli/Helmholtz acoustic tradition as the closed pipe — with both ends open (both antinodes), the air column supports all integer harmonics, unlike the closed pipe's odd-only restriction
fields.mnemonic:
“Open at both ends, welcomes every harmonic” — all integer harmonics are allowed, unlike the
closed pipe.
fields.example: L = 0.5 m, v = 340 m/s. Find the 2nd harmonic (n=2)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting all integers n are allowed here, unlike the closed-pipe case which permits only odd n.
• Mixing up the 2L denominator with the closed pipe's 4L.
• Ignoring end corrections at both open ends, which matter more here since there are two ends
 instead of one.

fields.title: Resonance in Closed pipe
fields.variables: f = Frequency of n-th harmonic,  n = Odd integer sequence (1, 3, 5...),  v = Speed of sound,  L = Effective acoustic length
fields.description: Resonance in closed pipes occurs when sound waves create standing waves, resulting in specific resonant frequencies determined by the pipe's length and the speed of sound.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing wind instruments such as flutes or organ pipes
fields.given_by: Rooted in Daniel Bernoulli's 18th-century studies of vibrating air columns, later systematized by Hermann von Helmholtz — a closed end forces a displacement node there, permitting only odd harmonics to resonate
fields.mnemonic: “Closed end, only odd friends” — a pipe closed at one end supports only odd harmonics.
fields.example: L = 0.5 m, v = 340 m/s. Find the fundamental frequency (n=1)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting only odd values of n (1, 3, 5…) are allowed — even harmonics simply don't exist in a
 closed pipe.
• Confusing 4L (closed pipe) with 2L (open pipe) in the denominator.
• Ignoring the small end correction in real pipes, which slightly increases the effective length
 beyond the measured L.

fields.title: de Broglie Wavelength
fields.variables: λ = de Broglie wavelength,  h = Planck's constant,  p = Linear momentum,  m = Mass,  v = Velocity
fields.description: The formula states that every particle, from electrons to larger objects, has an associated wavelength(λ) that is inversely proportional to its momentum(mv)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing electron microscopes, electron diffraction, or quantum mechanical wave behavior
fields.mnemonic: “Every moving mass hides a wave” — momentum, not just velocity, sets the wavelength
fields.example:
Electron: m = 9.1×10-31 kg, v = 1×106
m/s. Find λ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the denominator is momentum (mv), so at relativistic speeds the ordinary mv must
be replaced by relativistic momentum.
• Assuming this only applies to electrons — deBroglie's relation applies to any moving mass,
though the wavelength is only noticeable for very small masses.
• Confusing this matter-wavelength with a photon's wavelength formula — different physical
origin even though both use h.

fields.title: Energy of Photon
fields.variables: E = Photon energy,  h = Planck's constant; ν = Wave frequency,  c = Speed of light,   λ = Wavelength
fields.description: The energy of a photon is the energy carried by a single photon, which is directly proportional to its electromagnetic frequency(f) and inversely proportional to its wavelength. (λ)
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing photoelectric emission metrics, spectroscopy bands, or laser optics calculations
fields.mnemonic:
“Bluer light, bigger punch” — shorter wavelength or higher frequency means more energetic
photons
fields.example: λ = 500 nm. Find E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to convert λ from nm to m before dividing.
• Mixing up the two equivalent forms (hf vs hc/λ) and plugging frequency into the wavelength
 version by mistake.
• Forgetting to divide by 1.6×10-19 when a final answer is expected in eV rather than joules.

fields.title: Nuclear Binding Energy
fields.form: BE = (Z × m_p + N × m_n - M) × c^2
fields.variables: BE = Total nuclear binding energy,  Z = Total proton count,  m_p = Mass of protons,  N = Total neutron count,  m_n = Mass of neutrons,  M = Atomic mass,  c = Speed of light
fields.description: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to completely disassemble a nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons, reflecting the stability of the nucleus.
fields.when_to_use: When assessing structural isotopic decay stability timelines or computing macro energy outputs across stellar core cycles
fields.given_by: why a nucleus's mass is always slightly less than the sum of its separate protons and neutrons, with that "missing" mass converted into the energy holding the nucleus together
fields.mnemonic:
“The mass the nucleus “spent” to hold itself together” — that missing mass, converted to energy,
is the binding energy.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing binding energy (energy to disassemble a nucleus into nucleons) with the Q-value of a
specific reaction — related ideas, different quantities.
• Forgetting BE per nucleon (BE/A) is the more meaningful number for comparing nuclear
stability across elements, not total BE.
• Mixing up Z (protons) and N (neutrons) when the mass number A = Z+N is given instead of N
 directly.

fields.title: Q-value of Nuclear Reaction
fields.variables: Q = Total net energy released,  m_reactants,m_products = Mass of reactants and products
fields.description: The Q value of a nuclear reaction is the net energy released or absorbed, calculated from the mass difference between reactants(m_reactants) and products.(m_products)
fields.when_to_use: To determine if a nuclear fission/fusion reaction is exothermic or requires an external energy input threshold
fields.given_by: A direct application of Einstein's mass-energy equivalence (E = mc²) — quantifies the energy released or absorbed in a nuclear reaction based on the tiny but measurable difference in mass between reactants and products
fields.mnemonic: “Missing mass becomes energy” — whatever mass vanishes reappears as released energy.
fields.example:
Total reactant mass = 235.1230 u, 
total product mass = 235.1150 u. Find Q?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting masses must be in atomic mass units (u) for the 931.5 MeV/u conversion to apply
 directly.
• Getting the sign backwards — positive Q means energy is released (exothermic), negative Q
means energy must be supplied.
• Leaving out a particle (like a neutron or emitted particle) when totalling reactant or product
 mass.

fields.title: Rydberg Formula (spectral lines)
fields.variables: λ = Electromagnetic wavelength,  R = Rydberg constant,  Z = Atomic number,  n1 = Lower energy state,  n2 = Higher energy state
fields.description: The Rydberg formula predicts the wavelengths of spectral lines produced when an electron transitions between energy levels in a hydrogen atom.
fields.when_to_use: To map astronomical chemical properties via starlight emission analysis or checking quantum electronic transitions
fields.mnemonic:
“Bigger jump, bluer photon” — a larger gap between energy levels means a shorter, more
energetic wavelength.
fields.example:
Hydrogen (Z=1), Balmer series H_α: n1
=2, n2
=3, 
R_H
=1.097×10^7
 m^-1
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the Z² factor when working with hydrogen-like ions (He+, Li2+) rather than plain hydrogen.
• Swapping n1 and n2 — n1 is always the lower (final) level, n2 the higher (initial) level.
• Using this formula for multi-electron atoms, where it doesn't hold — it's exact only for single-electron (hydrogen-like) systems.

fields.title: Lens Formula
fields.variables: f = Focal length,  v = Image distance,  u = Object distance
fields.description: Relates object's distance, image distance and focal length for thin lenses. Converging lens has +ve focal length
fields.when_to_use: When calibrating camera focus sensors, slide projectors, or magnification glass modules
fields.mnemonic:
“Future minus past” — image distance v minus object distance u, following the Cartesian sign
convention.
fields.example:
Convex lens, f = 10 cm, u = −15 cm (real object). 
Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Mixing up the lens sign convention (1/f = 1/v − 1/u) with the mirror formula (1/f = 1/v + 1/u) —
they look similar but differ.
• Forgetting u is negative for a real object placed in front of the lens, by the standard Cartesian
convention.
• Forgetting f is positive for a converging (convex) lens and negative for a diverging (concave)
lens

fields.title: Magnification (mirror)
fields.variables: m = Magnification,  v = Image distance,  u = Object distance
fields.description: Ratio of image size to object size. (positive m= erect image, negative m= inverted image)
fields.when_to_use: When evaluating concave or convex reflective surfaces for rearview vehicle mirrors or vanity zoom reflections
fields.given_by: as the ratio of image height to object height — the negative sign in m = −v/u (using the standard sign convention) tells you whether the image is inverted (real) or upright (virtual)
fields.mnemonic:
“Negative means upright and virtual is the odd one out” — sign of m tells you image orientation
at a glance.
fields.example:
Concave mirror: u = −30 cm, v = −60 cm. 
Find magnification?
fields.answer: m = −\frac{(−60)}{(−30)} = −2 → image is inverted and twice the size
fields.common_mistakes:
• Dropping the negative sign in the formula — it's m = −v/u, and that sign carries real information about image orientation.
• Mixing up mirror sign convention (measured from the pole, with distances against incident light taken negative) with the lens sign convention —
 they're not identical.
• Forgetting |m| > 1 means magnified, |m| < 1 means diminished, and the sign (+ or −) separately tells you upright vs inverted.

fields.title: Lens Maker's Formula
fields.variables: f = Resultant focal length,  n = Glass core index scale,  R_1 = Curvature radius of front face,  R_2 = Curvature radius of back face
fields.description: Used to calculate focal length of a lens from its physical dimensions and refractive index.
fields.when_to_use: To grind exact custom corrective eyeglass optics or precision industrial camera zoom assemblies
fields.given_by: mathematical foundation behind lens manufacturing — tells opticians exactly how to grind a lens's curvature and choose its material to achieve a specific focal length or power
fields.mnemonic:
“Shape times material” — focal length depends on both how curved the surfaces are and how
much the material bends light.
fields.example:
A converging lens: n = 1.5, R1
= 20 cm, R2
= −20 cm. Find f?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Getting the sign convention for R1 and R2 wrong — radii are positive if the centre of curvature is on the outgoing side, negative otherwise 
(Cartesian convention).
• Forgetting n here is the refractive index of the lens material relative to the surrounding
medium, not an absolute value.
• Mixing up R1 (first surface light hits) and 
R2(second surface) when the lens is asymmetric.

fields.title: Power of a Lens
fields.variables: P = Optical refractive power,  f = Focal length
fields.description: Power measures the ability of a lens to converge or diverge light. Opticians use dipotre to prescribe spectacles
fields.when_to_use: When formulating medical optometry prescriptions, focusing telescope clusters, or consumer glass lens sets
fields.given_by: Introduced by opticians in the 19th century as a practical way to describe lens strength — defined as the reciprocal of focal length, so a more "powerful" lens bends light more sharply over a shorter distance
fields.mnemonic:
“Short focal length, strong lens” — power is just the reciprocal of focal length, so smaller f
means bigger P.
fields.example: A lens has f = 0.25 m. Find its power?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting f must be in metres for P to come out in dioptres — a very common unit slip.
• Forgetting sign convention: converging (convex) lenses have positive P, diverging (concave)
lenses have negative P.
• Adding powers of lenses in contact without first confirming they're thin and in direct contact
(Pnet = P1+P2 only holds under that assumption).

fields.title: Young's Double Slit Experiment
fields.variables: β = Fringe width,  λ = Wavelength,   D = Distance to viewing screen,  d = Width spacing separating source slits
fields.description: In YDSE, equally spaced bright and dark fringes are formaed on screen due to interference of light.
fields.when_to_use: To calculate micro physical features of light or execute precise structural slit gauge testing metrics
fields.mnemonic:
“Big D on top, small d below” — fringes spread out with screen distance and squeeze together
with slit separation.
fields.example: λ = 589 nm, D = 1.2 m, d = 0.5 mm. Find fringe width?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Swapping D (slit-to-screen distance) and d (slit separation) — similar letters, very different scales.
• Leaving λ in nm while D and d are in m or mm — convert everything to one consistent unit first.
• Forgetting fringe width is the same for every fringe (uniform spacing) — only true because θ is small in this setup.

fields.title: Conditions for Bright/Dark Fringes
fields.variables: Δ = Optical path difference,  n = Fringe order,  λ = Monochromatic wavelength
fields.description: Bright fringes forms when path difference(Δ) is mutiple of λ and Dark fringes froms when path difference(Δ) is multiple of λ/2
fields.when_to_use: When debugging interferometer alignments, thin film oil glare layouts, or laser testing patterns
fields.mnemonic:
“Whole steps light up, half-steps cancel out” — path difference in whole wavelengths gives
constructive interference, half-wavelengths give destructive
fields.example: λ = 600 nm. Find the path difference for the 2nd dark fringe (n=2)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the dark-fringe condition uses (2n−1), not just n, in the numerator.
• Miscounting fringe order — n=1 for dark fringes corresponds to Δ = λ/2, the very first dark band off-centre.
• Mixing up path difference Δ (in metres) with phase difference (in radians) — they're related by a factor of 2π/λ, not identical.

fields.title: Diffraction Grating
fields.variables: d = Grating slit spacing parameter,  θ= Angular dispersion deflection,  n = Principal spectral order,  λ = Target optical wavelength
fields.description: A diffraction grating has many slits. Each wavelength is diffracted at different angles, seperating colors.
fields.when_to_use: To engineer spectrometer instruments, chemical emission spectrum trackers, or high-accuracy optical wave dividers
fields.mnemonic:
“Same form as YDSE bright fringes, but d is now the grating spacing” — more slits, sharper
maxima, same underlying condition.
fields.example: d = 1/5000 cm (grating), λ = 600 nm. Find θ for the first-order maximum (n=1)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting d here is the distance between adjacent slits in the grating, often given as “lines
per cm” that must first be inverted.
• Confusing this with the single-slit minima condition, which looks similar but describes dark
 fringes, not bright ones.
• Forgetting higher orders (larger n) may not exist if sinθ would have to exceed 1 — always
 check nature is possible.

fields.title: Brewster's Law
fields.variables: θ_B = Brewster's angle,  n_2, n_1 = Refractive indices of medium 2 ,1
fields.description: At Brewster's angle, reflected ligth is completely plane-polarized
fields.when_to_use: When manufacturing anti-glare coatings, specialized laser windows, or polarization prisms
fields.mnemonic:
“The angle where reflected light becomes perfectly polarized” — tangent, not sine, is what
connects θ_B
 to the refractive index ratio.
fields.example:
Light goes from air (n1
=1) to glass (n2
=1.5). 
Find Brewster's angle?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using sin instead of tan — easy to confuse with Snell's law, which does use sine.
• Forgetting at Brewster's angle, the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to eachother.
• Mixing up n1and n2 — the ratio direction matters for which angle you're solving for.

fields.title: Malus's Law
fields.variables: I = Output light beam intensity,  I_0 = Initial polarized incoming intensity,  θ = Vector offset angle between polarization axes
fields.description: Malus’ law states that the intensity(I) of plane-polarized light passing through an analyzer varies as the square of the cosine(cos^2 θ) of the angle between the polarizer and analyzer axes.
fields.when_to_use: When configuring adjustable optical filters, liquid crystal displays, or specialized polarization tracking lenses
fields.mnemonic:
“Aligned = full light, crossed = none” — intensity through a polarizer follows a cosine-squared
curve as the analyzer rotates.
fields.example:
I
_0
 = 100 W/m², θ = 30° between polarizer and analyzer axes. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting it's cos²θ, not cosθ — a very common slip.
• Forgetting at θ = 90° (crossed polarizers), intensity is exactly zero, not just reduced.
• Applying Malus's law to unpolarized light passing through the first polarizer — that step
instead uses I = I0/2, since Malus's law only governs the second polarizer onward.

fields.title: Acceleration due to Gravity (surface)
fields.variables: g = Acceleration due to gravity,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Planetary mass,  R = Planetary radius
fields.description: Gravitational accleration at surface of a planet of mass M and radius R
fields.when_to_use: When setting standard planetary mass weight configurations or foundational gravity reference frameworks
fields.mnemonic: “Why apples fall at 9.8” — this is Newton's law of gravitation applied at the planet's own surface.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting g is not truly constant — it varies slightly with latitude, altitude, and local density variations.
• Using diameter instead of radius R by mistake.
• Forgetting this specific formula only applies exactly at the surface (r = R); elsewhere, use E_g=GM/r² with the general r.

fields.title: Variation of g with Height
fields.variables: g_h = Variation of g with height h,  g = Acceleration due to gravity,  h = Height distance above planet's surface,  R = Planetary radius
fields.description: The acceleration due to gravity decreases as increase in height above surface of earth (h << R)
fields.when_to_use: For low-orbit atmosphere tracking loops, aerospace altitude calibrations, or mountain-scale gravity anomalies
fields.given_by: g decreases going upward because distance from Earth's center increases, but also decreases going downward because the effective mass pulling you shrinks (only the mass within your radius contributes)
fields.mnemonic:
“Going up costs twice as much as going down” — the height formula has a factor of 2 that the
depth formula doesn't.
fields.example: g = 9.8 m/s², h = 32 km, R = 6400 km. Find g_h?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this approximation is only valid for h ≪ R — for large h, the exact inverse-square formula 
g_h = GM/(R+h)² must be used instead.
• Dropping the factor of 2 and accidentally using the depth-variation formula instead.
• Forgetting g decreases going up but increases going down (up to the surface) — the two formulas trend oppositely near R.

fields.title: Variation of g with depth
fields.variables: g_d = Variation of g with depth d,  g = Acceleration due to gravity,  d = Depth distance,  R = Total planet radius
fields.description: Gradual decrease in g due to increasing depth
fields.when_to_use: To design subsurface geological instruments, drilling structural nodes, or analyze planetary interior mass pressures
fields.given_by: g decreases going upward because distance from Earth's center increases, but also decreases going downward because the effective mass pulling you shrinks (only the mass within your radius contributes)
fields.mnemonic:
“Dig down, gravity thins out” — g decreases linearly as you go deeper, reaching zero at the
centre.
fields.example: g = 9.8 m/s², d = 1600 km, R = 6400 km. Find g_d?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this formula assumes uniform density throughout the planet — real planets (like
Earth) don't perfectly follow it.
• Mixing this up with the height formula, which uses a factor of 2 in front of h that this one doesn't have.
• Forgetting g_d= 0 exactly at the centre (d = R), not at the surface.

fields.title: Gravitational Potential Energy
fields.variables: U = Gravitational potential energy,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Planetary mass,  m = Object mass,  r = Seperation between planet center and object's center
fields.description: The GPE formula depicts the potential energy between two masses(M, m) away at a distance of r.
fields.when_to_use: When computing multi-body flight tracking metrics, deep ballistic escape mechanics, or planetary launch power budgets
fields.given_by: multiplying gravitational potential (energy per unit mass) by the actual mass placed in the field — giving the total potential energy of a two-body gravitational system
fields.mnemonic:
“V times the mass you place there” — U is just gravitational potential scaled up by the object's
own mass
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the negative sign — it reflects an attractive force, and U increases (becomes less
negative) as r increases.
• Confusing this with the simpler U = mgh, which is only a local approximation valid near a
planet's surface for small heights.
• Using the object's weight rather than its mass m in the formula.

fields.title: Gravitational Potential
fields.variables: V = Gravitational potential,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Planetary mass,  r = Planetary radius
fields.description: The gravitational potential(V) is a scalar potential associating with each point in space the work (energy transferred) per unit mass to bring a test mass from infinity to point at distance r.
fields.when_to_use: To chart energy contour fields or establish foundational baseline acceleration levels across macroscopic space lines
fields.given_by: the work done per unit mass to bring an object from infinity to a point in a gravitational field, with the negative sign showing that gravity always does positive work as objects fall inward
fields.mnemonic:
“Potential energy per kilogram, always negative” — zero only at infinity, and grows more
negative as you get closer to the mass.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing gravitational potential V (J/kg, a property of the point in space) with gravitational
 potential energy U = mV (J, a property of a specific mass placed there).
• Forgetting the negative sign — gravitational potential is always ≤ 0, unlike electric potential
 which can be positive or negative.
• Forgetting V → 0 only as r → ∞, so it's never actually zero at any finite distance.

fields.title: Orbital Velocity
fields.variables: v_o = Orbital velocity,  G = Universial gravitational constant,  M = Planetary mass,  r = Planetary radius/ axial distance
fields.description: Velocity required for a satellite to maintain a circular orbit of radius r
fields.when_to_use: When launching or locking a satellite device into a permanently sustained circular altitude profile
fields.given_by: imagining a projectile fired fast enough that it continuously falls around the Earth instead of hitting the ground, tracing out a stable orbit
fields.mnemonic:
“Fall forever, but sideways” — orbital velocity is exactly the speed needed so that the satellite's
fall matches the planet's curvature.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting r is the orbital radius from the centre of the planet, not the altitude above the surface.
• Confusing orbital velocity with escape velocity (which is √2 times larger, v_e = √(2GM/r)).
• Assuming v_o is independent of r — it actually decreases as r increases.

fields.title: Kepler's Third Law
fields.variables: T = Full cyclic orbital period duration,  r = Mean orbital radius coordinate profile
fields.description: Square of orbital period is proportional to cube of semi-major axis
fields.when_to_use: When scaling structural harmonic tracking systems across planetary loops, exoplanet discoveries, or star-system setups
fields.mnemonic: “Farther out, disproportionately slower” — orbital period grows faster than orbital radius.
fields.example:
Planet A orbits at r,  planet B orbits at 4r. 
Compare their time periods?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting it's a proportionality, not an equation with a fixed constant — the constant depends
 on the central mass being orbited.
• Mixing up which power goes with which variable: T is squared, r is cubed — easy to swap
 under pressure.
• Applying the same proportionality constant across two different central bodies (e.g. comparing
a moon of Jupiter to a moon of Earth) without adjusting for the different masses.

fields.title: Total Energy of Satellite
fields.variables: E = Total energy,  G = Universal gravitational constant,  M = Planetary mass,  m = Mass of satellite,  r = Distance between planet and satellite
fields.description: Total Mechanical energy(KE + PE) of a satellite in circular orbit.
fields.when_to_use: To assess overall orbit structural safety boundaries, decay tracking metrics, or orbital escape step requirements
fields.given_by: combination of satellite's kinetic and gravitational potential energy to show that its total energy is always negative, meaning it remains bound to the planet
fields.mnemonic:
“Always negative, always bound” — the minus sign says the satellite is gravitationally trapped in
orbit.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the negative sign — dropping it changes the physical meaning from “bound” to "unbound.”
• Forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator, unlike gravitational PE which has no such factor.
• Confusing this total energy with just the kinetic or just the potential energy of the satellite —it's KE + PE combined.

fields.title: Gravitational Field Intensity
fields.variables: E_g = Gravitational field strength vector,  G = Gravitational constant,  M = Planet mass,  r = Radial distance vector
fields.description: Gravitational force(E_g) experienced per unit mass at distance r from source of mass M
fields.when_to_use: To map spatial acceleration fields around planet zones, satellite stations, or localized celestial structural matrices
fields.given_by: direct consequence of Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation — describes the gravitational force experienced per unit mass at a point in space, independent of the mass placed there
fields.mnemonic:
“Same shape as g, because it is g” — gravitational field intensity is just the acceleration due to
gravity at a point
fields.example:
M = 6×10^24 kg (Earth), r = 6.4×10^6
m. Find E
_g?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting r is measured from the centre of the mass, not from its surface.
• Mixing up units N/kg (field intensity) with m/s² (acceleration) — they're numerically identical
but conceptually distinct.
• Forgetting the inverse-square dependence — doubling r quarters E_g, not just halves it.

fields.title: Second Equation of Motion
fields.variables: s = Total linear displacement,  u = Initial velocity,  t = Time,  a = Constant acceleration
fields.description: Displacement of a body under constant acceleration(a) in terms of time(t).
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the exact dynamic positional clearance or braking distance under continuous constant acceleration
fields.given_by: the first  equation of motion— expresses how the linear displacement relates directly to  constant acceleration
fields.mnemonic:
“Steady part plus the extra push” — ut is the distance you'd cover at constant speed, ½at² is the
bonus/loss from acceleration.
fields.example: u = 4 m/s, a = 3 m/s², t = 2 s. Find s?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the ½ factor in front of at².
• Squaring t incorrectly or forgetting to square it at all.
• Using final velocity v instead of initial velocity u in this formula — it specifically requires u

fields.title: Third Equation of Motion
fields.variables: v = Final veloicity,  u = Initial velocity,  a = Constant acceleration,  s = Total linear displacement
fields.description: Relation between final velocity(v), initial velocity(u), acceleration(a) and displacement(s)
fields.when_to_use: When tracking moving bodies undergoing uniform acceleration where the time parameter is entirely omitted or unmeasured
fields.given_by: combining the first two equations of motion to eliminate time (t) — expresses how final velocity relates directly to displacement under constant acceleration
fields.mnemonic: “The one without time” — useful exactly when a problem doesn't mention or ask about time.
fields.example: u = 5 m/s, a = 2 m/s², s = 10 m. Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to take the square root at the end — the formula gives v², not v directly.
• Using this equation when the question actually gives or asks for time — the first or second
equation of motion is more direct then.
• Sign errors with a when the object is decelerating — deceleration means a is negative relative
to the direction of motion.

fields.title: Average Velocity
fields.variables: v_avg = Average velocity,  Δx = Net displacement vector,  Δt = Total time interval
fields.description: Average velocity is gives as ratio of total displacement by total time taken
fields.when_to_use: When calculating the overall rate of position change over a discrete macro time frame without tracking instant variations
fields.given_by: Rooted in Galilean relativity — the principle, described by Galileo Galilei, that motion can only be measured relative to a chosen frame of reference, not in absolute terms
fields.mnemonic:
“Where you ended up, over how long it took” — average velocity only cares about net
displacement, not the path taken.
fields.example:
A runner moves from x = 2 m to x = 22 m in 4 s. 
Find v_avg?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing average velocity (uses net displacement) with average speed (uses total distance
travelled) — they differ whenever the path isn't a straight line in one direction.
• Forgetting Δx can be negative if the object ends up behind where it started.
• Assuming average velocity equals the velocity at the midpoint of the time interval — it
doesn't, unless acceleration is constant.

fields.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
fields.variables: p_final = Final momentum,  p_initial = Initial momentum
fields.description: It explains how, in the absence of external forces, the total momentum of a system remains unchanged, even when objects within the system interact, collide, or exchange forces.
fields.when_to_use: Standard primary analysis step used when solving mechanical impact, explosion, or ballistic interaction setups
fields.given_by: since every action has an equal and opposite reaction, the total momentum of an isolated system remains unchanged, regardless of internal collisions or interactions
fields.mnemonic:
“No outside push, no momentum change” — total momentum before an interaction equals total
momentum after, provided no external force acts.
fields.example:
Two carts: m1
= 2 kg at 3 m/s collides with m2
= 1 kg at rest; they stick together. Find common
 velocity v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this only holds when no net external force acts on the system — friction or gravity
from outside breaks the conservation.
• Losing track of direction (sign) when objects move toward each other — momentum is a
vector.
• Confusing conservation of momentum (always true in an isolated system) with conservation of
kinetic energy (only true in elastic collisions).

fields.title: Coefficient of Restitution
fields.variables: e = Coefficient of restitution e(0,1) [0- perfectly inelastic, 1- perfectly elastic],  v2, v1 = Final velocities after collision,  u1, u2 = Initial speed before collision
fields.description: The coefficient of restitution (COR) is a dimensionless measure of how elastic a collision is, defined as the ratio of relative velocity after collision to relative velocity before collision.
fields.when_to_use: To model bounce behaviors, kinetic energy drops, and rebound velocities during mechanical collision profiles
fields.given_by: an empirical measure of how "bouncy" or elastic a collision is, based on the ratio of relative velocities after and before impact
fields.mnemonic:
“Separation over approach” — e compares how fast objects fly apart after a collision to how fast
they came together before it.
fields.example:
Two balls collide: u1= 5 m/s, u2 = 0, after collision 
v1= 1 m/s, v2= 3 m/s. Find e?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting e = 1 means perfectly elastic, e = 0 means perfectly inelastic (objects stick together) — 
e is always between 0 and 1.
• Swapping numerator and denominator — it's velocity of separation over velocity of approach,
not the reverse.
• Mixing up sign conventions for objects moving in opposite directions — pick one positive
direction and stay consistent.

fields.title: Work done by a Force
fields.variables: W = Total work done,  F = Force applied,  s = Linear displacement,  θ = Angle between force and direction vectors
fields.description: Work(W) is done only when a force(F) causes displacement(s) in direction of the force.
fields.when_to_use: To track system energy changes or solve for structural velocity updates through the Work-Energy Theorem
fields.given_by: only the component of force acting along the direction of motion contributes to the work done
fields.mnemonic:
“Only the part of the force along the path counts” — cosθ projects F onto the direction of
displacement.
fields.example: F = 20 N, s = 5 m, θ = 60° between force and displacement. Find W?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting θ = 90° gives zero work — a force perpendicular to displacement does no work at
all.
• Using the angle between two forces instead of the angle between force and displacement.
• Forgetting work is negative when θ > 90° (e.g. friction opposing motion) — not just smaller,
but negative.

fields.title: Kinetic Energy
fields.variables: KE = Kinetic energy,  m = Mass,  v = Velocity/Linear speed
fields.description: Energy(KE) possessed by a body due to its motion
fields.when_to_use: Standard block use across collision evaluations, trajectory paths, and orbital balance
fields.mnemonic: “Speed matters twice as much” — KE grows with the square of velocity, not velocity itself.
fields.example: m = 2 kg, v = 3 m/s. Find KE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the ½ factor at the front — a very common slip.
• Forgetting KE scales with v², so doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, not just doubles it.
• Using momentum (mv) formulas interchangeably with kinetic energy formulas — they behave
very differently with velocity.

fields.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy
fields.variables: KE = Kinetic energy,  PE = Potential energy
fields.description: Total Mechanical energy(kinetic + potential) remains constant in absence of non-conservative forces.
fields.when_to_use: To find positions or velocities for falling bodies or conservative pendulum structures without modeling explicit complex accelerations
fields.given_by: A cornerstone of classical mechanics, formalized through the 18th and 19th centuries as physicists recognized that kinetic and potential energy can convert into each other while their sum remains unchanged — provided no energy is lost to friction or air resistance
fields.mnemonic:
“Energy just changes costume” — kinetic and potential trade off, but their sum stays the same
(no friction/air resistance).
fields.example:
A ball falls from height h = 5 m (starts at rest). Just before hitting the ground (h = 0):
Initial: KE = 0, PE = mgh. Final: PE = 0, so KE = mgh = m×10×5 = 50m J
fields.common_mistakes:
• Applying this when friction or air resistance is present — mechanical energy is only conserved
in the absence of non-conservative forces.
• Forgetting to choose a consistent reference level for PE = 0 before comparing two points.
• Ignoring other energy forms (heat, sound) in problems that explicitly mention losses — total
energy is still conserved, but not purely mechanical energy.

fields.title: Efficiency of a Machine
fields.variables: η = Mechanical efficiency,  W_output = Work output,  W_input = Work input
fields.description: Efficiency of a machine is the ratio of work done(W_output) to total work input(W_input), expressed as percentage
fields.when_to_use: When quantifying the structural optimization limit inside mechaical linkages
fields.given_by: since no real machine is perfectly lossless, efficiency quantifies the gap between energy supplied and useful energy delivered
fields.mnemonic:
“What you get out, over what you put in” — always less than 100% once friction and losses are
real.
fields.example: W_input = 500 J, W_output = 350 J. Find η?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting η can never exceed 100% for any real machine — getting a number above 100%
signals an arithmetic error.
• Swapping input and output work in the ratio.
• Forgetting to multiply by 100 when the answer is expected as a percentage rather than a
decimal fraction.

fields.title: Wave Speed
fields.variables: v = Wave speed,  f = Linear frequency,  λ = Physical wavelength
fields.description: Speed of a wave(v) depends on frequency(f) by which the wave oscillates and the wavelength(λ).
fields.when_to_use: To resolve wavelength spacings or propagation metrics across variable density phase bounds
fields.given_by: Follows directly from the basic distance-time relation — since a wave travels one wavelength (λ) in one time period (T), speed is simply λ divided by T, or equivalently f × λ.
fields.mnemonic: “How fast times how long, per cycle” — speed is simply frequency multiplied by wavelength.
fields.example: f = 500 Hz, λ = 0.68 m (sound in air). Find v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting that for a given medium, v is fixed — so if λ changes, f must change to compensate,
and vice versa.
• Using the wrong wave speed for the medium (e.g. speed of sound in air vs water vs a string).
• Mixing up wavelength units (cm vs m) before multiplying.

fields.title: Time Period
fields.variables: T = Standard time peiod,  f = Linear frequnecy
fields.description: The time period(T) is a reciprocal of frequency(f)
fields.when_to_use: Maps step linking cycle rates to raw frequency
fields.given_by: Simply the reciprocal of frequency — defined as the time taken to complete one full cycle of oscillation or wave motion
fields.mnemonic:
“Period and frequency are mirror images” — one measures time per cycle, the other cycles per
time.
fields.example: f = 4 Hz. Find T?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting T and f are simple reciprocals — no need to memorize a separate formula for one if
you know the other.
• Mixing up units — T is always in seconds, f always in hertz (1/s).
• Confusing time period of oscillation with “half-life” or other unrelated time constants that
sound similar.

fields.title: Angular Frequency
fields.variables: ω = Angular frequency,  f = Linear frequency,  T = Time period
fields.description: Angular frequency of a periodic wave in terms of frequeny(f) or time period(T)
fields.when_to_use: Universal conversion block linking standard time domain to sinusoidal phase components
fields.given_by: Defined as a way to express frequency in terms of radians rather than cycles — useful because it simplifies the mathematics of oscillatory and circular motion
fields.mnemonic:
“Full circle, every cycle” — one oscillation sweeps through 2π radians, so ω is just that scaled by
how many cycles happen per second.
fields.example: f = 50 Hz. Find ω?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing ω (rad/s) with f (Hz, cycles/s) — they differ by a factor of 2π.
• Forgetting T and f are reciprocals, so ω = 2π/T works exactly like ω = 2πf.
• Using ω directly as if it were a frequency in formulas that specifically expect f.

fields.title: Wave Number
fields.variables: k = Wave number,  λ = Fundamental wavelength
fields.description: Number of complete wave cycles per unit length, also called propagation constant.
fields.when_to_use: To set parameter metrics inside progressive sinusoidal phase engines
fields.given_by: Defined as a convenient way to express how rapidly a wave's phase changes with distance — introduced as the spatial counterpart to angular frequency (ω) in wave equations
fields.mnemonic: “How many radians per metre” — wave number is angular frequency's spatial twin.
fields.example: λ = 2 m. Find k?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing wave number k (rad/m) with the “spectroscopic” wave number (1/λ, no 2π) used in
some chemistry contexts.
• Mixing up k with the spring constant or Boltzmann constant, which share the same letter.
• Forgetting the units are radians per metre, not just “per metre”.

fields.title: Equation of Progressive Wave
fields.variables: y = Particle displacement,  A = Amplitude,  ω = Angular frequency,  t = Time,  k = Wave number,  x = Distance point
fields.description: Displacement(y) of a particle in a transverse progressive wave at position(x) and time(t)
fields.units: y (m),  A (m),  ω (\frac{rad}{s}),  t (s),  k (\frac{rad}{m}),   x (m)
fields.when_to_use: When looking to establish spatial phase values for standard acoustic or seismic propagating disturbances
fields.given_by: Rooted in the wave equation formalized by Jean le Rond d'Alembert in the 18th century, describing how a disturbance propagates through space and time
fields.mnemonic:
“Time pushes forward, position pulls back” — the minus sign in front of kx is what makes the
wave travel in the +x direction.
fields.example:
A = 0.05 m, ω = 4 rad/s, k = 2 rad/m. Find y at t = 1 s, 
x = 0.5 m.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using a + sign for a wave meant to travel in the +x direction — that actually describes a wave
moving in −x.
• Forgetting ωt and kx must both be in radians, not degrees, inside the sine function.
• Confusing k (wave number, rad/m) with the spring constant k — same symbol, completely
different physical quantity.

fields.title: Intensity of a Wave
fields.variables: I = Wave intensity,  ρ = Medium density,  v = Wave speed,  ω = Angular frequency,  A = Amplitude
fields.description: Power(I) transmitted per unit area by a mechanical wave
fields.when_to_use: To track attenuation drop levels or power transfers through medium transitions
fields.given_by: Describes how the power carried by a wave is distributed over the surface it passes through — a fundamental measure of wave "strength" independent of the source's total output
fields.mnemonic: “Intensity loves squares” — it grows with the square of both amplitude and angular frequency.
fields.example:
ρ = 1.2 kg/m³ (air), v = 340 m/s, ω = 100 rad/s, 
A=  0.01 m. Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting intensity scales with A², so doubling amplitude quadruples intensity, not just
 doubles it.
• Using frequency f instead of angular frequency 
ω = 2πf directly in the formula.
• Forgetting ρ and v here refer to the density and wave speed of the medium the wave travels
through, not the source.

fields.title: Transistor Current Relation
fields.variables: I_E = Total emitter current,  I_B = Base current,  I_C = Collector current
fields.description: The emitter current(I_E) in a transistor splits into base(I_B) and collector(I_C) currents.
fields.when_to_use: Universal base formula used to link structural branches across all operational BJT models
fields.given_by: A direct consequence of charge conservation — since a transistor has only three terminals, whatever current enters the base and collector must exit through the emitter
fields.mnemonic:
“What goes in, must come out” — simple Kirchhoff's current law applied to the three transistor
terminals.
fields.example:
I
_B
 = 0.1 mA, I_C
 = 4.9 mA. Find I_E?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this is just current conservation (KCL) — no need to memorize it separately once
 you know that.
• Mixing up which current is largest — IE
 is always the biggest of the three, IB
  the smallest.
• Using this relation with the wrong sign convention for a PNP transistor, where conventional
current directions flip.

fields.title: Current Amplification Factor (Beta)
fields.variables: β = Common-emitter current gain,  ΔI_C = Collector current  variation,  ΔI_B = Base current variation
fields.description: Measures how much the collector(IC) current changes for a small change in base(IB) current.
fields.when_to_use: Essential to evaluate dc load bias setups or small-signal amplifier staging
fields.given_by: While characterizing carrier flow between the emitter, base, and collector, Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley at Bell Laboratories also derived this gain parameter — the common-emitter counterpart to Alpha
fields.mnemonic:
“Beta is Big” — in common-emitter mode, a tiny base current controls a much larger collector
current, so β is typically in the tens to hundreds.
fields.example:
ΔIC
 = 4.9 mA, ΔIB
 = 0.1 mA. Find β?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting β has no upper bound in principle (unlike α, which is always < 1).
• Mixing up numerator and denominator — it's collector current over base current, not the
reverse.
• Assuming β is a fixed constant for a transistor — in reality it varies with temperature and
operating current

fields.title: Current Amplification Factor (Alpha)
fields.variables: α = Common-base current gain,  ΔI_C = Change in collector loop current,  ΔI_E = Change in emitter line current
fields.description: Ratio of collector current(IC) to emitter current(IE) in common-base configuration; always slightly less than 1.
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing small signals performance boundaries iniside common-base transistor arrays
fields.given_by: Formalized by Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley at Bell Labs while studying carrier movement from emitter to collector
fields.mnemonic:
“Alpha is Almost 1” — in common-base configuration, collector current is nearly all of the
emitter current, so α is always just under 1.
fields.example:
ΔIC
 = 4.9 mA, ΔIE
 = 5 mA. Find α?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Expecting α to sometimes exceed 1 — it never does, since IC is always slightly less than IE
• Confusing α (common-base gain) with β (common-emitter gain) — they describe different configurations.
• Using total currents IC, IE instead of small-signal changes ΔIC, ΔIE  where the question specifies
 AC gain.

fields.title: Relation between Alpha and Beta
fields.variables: α = Common-base amplification gain,   β = Common-emitter current gain
fields.description: Connects the two current gain definitions of a transistor
fields.when_to_use: To switch transistor parameter metrices when re-configuring topology models
fields.given_by: Kirchhoff's Current Law, which states that the emitter current I_{E} is the sum of the collector current I_{C} and base current I_{B}
fields.mnemonic:
“α close to 1 makes β explode” — as α approaches 1, the denominator shrinks toward zero and
β shoots up
fields.example: α = 0.98. Find β?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the inverse relation α = β/(1+β) also holds — useful for going the other direction.
• Plugging in α > 1, which is physically impossible since α is always slightly less than 1.
• Assuming β changes linearly with α — it's highly non-linear near α = 1.

fields.title: Diode Equation
fields.variables: I = Net diode current,  I_0 = Initial diode current, V = Total voltage,  V_T = Thermal voltage
fields.description: Describes the exponential current-voltage relationship of a p-n junction
fields.when_to_use: When modelling logarithmic conduction curves or determining dynamic  resistance changes for solid state junctions
fields.mnemonic:
“Exception current times an exponential kick” — tiny leakage current I0
 gets exponentially
amplified once V exceeds V_T
fields.example: I_0 = 1×10^-12 A, V = 0.6V,  V_T = 0.026V (roomtemperature). Find I?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature (300 K) — it changes with temperature.

• Dropping the “−1” term, which matters for small or reverse V but is negligible once V ≫ VT

• Forgetting this models an ideal diode — real diodes include a non-ideality factor n, giving VT→nVT

fields.title: Half-Wave Rectifier Efficiency
fields.variables: η = Conversion efficiency,  P_dc = DC output power,  P_ac = AC input power
fields.description: Maximum theoretical efficiency of coverting AC to DC using half-wave rectifier
fields.when_to_use: To measure fundamental maximum power conversion inside asymmetric half-wave circuits
fields.given_by: the fundamental laws of Alternating Current (AC) and Direct Current (DC) power
fields.mnemonic: “Half the wave, (roughly) half the full-wave efficiency” — 40.6% is almost exactly half of 81.2%
fields.example:
Like the full-wave case, this is the fixed theoretical maximum for an ideal half-wave rectifier with
a purely resistive load — it isn't computed from problem-specific numbers
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting only one half-cycle is used, so a large share of the input AC power is simply wasted.
• Confusing this with ripple factor (≈ 1.21) — different quantities entirely.
• Assuming this improves with a smoothing capacitor — it doesn't change this theoretical
efficiency figure.

fields.title: Full-Wave Rectifier Efficiency
fields.variables: η = Conversion efficiency,  P_dc = DC output power,  P_ac = AC input power
fields.description: Maximum theoretical efficiency of a full-wave rectifier, double the half-wave case
fields.when_to_use: To compute structural power conversion boundaries across center-tapped or bridge  rectifiers
fields.given_by: using fundamental principles of alternating and direct current first established by foundational scientists like Michael Faraday and later adapted for semiconductors
fields.mnemonic: “Full-wave uses both halves of the cycle” — roughly double the half-wave efficiency.
fields.example:
This is a fixed theoretical maximum for an ideal full-wave rectifier with resistive load — no
numbers to plug in, but it's derived from η = (0.812) using the ratio of DC power delivered to
total AC input power
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting this 81.2% is a theoretical ceiling for an ideal diode — real efficiency is always
somewhat lower.
• Mixing this figure up with the ripple factor (0.48) — they measure completely different things.
• Assuming efficiency changes with load resistance — for an ideal resistive load it stays fixed at
this value.

fields.title: Ripple Factor (Half-Wave)
fields.variables: γ = Ripple factor, I_rms = RMS value of AC components, I_dc = Average DC output current
fields.description: Measures the residual AC component in rectified DC output
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing and sizing filter components to handle high pulsating variations of half-wave rectification networks
fields.given_by: It quantifies the unwanted AC fluctuations remaining in a DC output
fields.mnemonic:
“Half the wave, more than double the ripple” — half-wave rectification leaves large gaps, so γ is
much higher.
fields.example:
For an ideal half-wave rectifier, Vrms
/Vdc = π/2:
fields.common_mistakes:
• Quoting 0.48 by mistake — that's the full-wave value, not half-wave.
• Forgetting this formula assumes an ideal diode and resistive load, with no smoothing
capacitor.
• Treating a smaller γ as automatically “more power” — it measures smoothness of DC, not
power delivered.

fields.title: Ripple Factor (Full-Wave)
fields.variables: γ = Unfiltered Ripple metric factor; I_rms = Root-mean-square variation load path current; I_dc = Fixed baseline stable average direct current target
fields.description: Full-Wave recitifiers gives smooth output than half-wave.
fields.when_to_use: Use to analyze smoothing filtering parameters across bridge rectifiers and power supply networks
fields.given_by: the ratio of the RMS value of the AC ripple component to the average DC value
fields.mnemonic: “Full-wave is far smoother — ripple factor drops to less than half of half-wave's.”
fields.example:
For an ideal full-wave rectifier, the ratio Vrms
/Vdc works out such that?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting γ is dimensionless — it's a ratio, not a voltage.
• Mixing up which rectifier (half-wave vs full-wave) a given γ value belongs to (0.48 vs 1.21).
• Assuming a larger filter capacitor changes this theoretical value — this γ is for the unfiltered
output; filtering reduces the practical ripple separately.

fields.title: Voltage Gain of Amplifier
fields.variables: A_v = System Voltage gain parameter;    V_o = Output terminal load load;  V_i= Source input network resistance,  β = Common-emitter current,  R_L = Load resistance,  I_in = Input current
fields.description: Ratio of output volatge(V_out) to input voltage(V_in) in a transistor amplifier circuit
fields.when_to_use: Use to quantify direct signal amplification performance inside standard active transistor circuits
fields.given_by: the small-signal equivalent circuit of the amplifier
fields.mnemonic: “Current gain borrows the load, divided by what it took to drive the input.”
fields.example:
β = 100, R_L
 = 2 kΩ, R_in = 1 kΩ. Find A_v?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing Rin (the amplifier's input resistance) with the source or load resistance.
• Forgetting the negative sign convention in common-emitter configurations (output is
inverted).
• Treating Av
 as constant across all frequencies — real amplifiers roll off at high/low frequencies.

fields.title: Power Gain of Amplifier
fields.variables: A_p = Total circuit power gain, β = Alternating current transistor factor; R_o = Load circuit resistance output track; R_i = Entry terminal input resistance path
fields.description: Combines current gain(β) and ratio of resistance to give overall power amplification(A_p)
fields.when_to_use: Use to establish full operational power efficiency factors across small signal stages.
fields.given_by: an external DC power supply (such as a battery or AC-to-DC mains adapter)
fields.mnemonic:
“Current gain squared, times the resistance trade” — power gain rides on β² because power
involves both extra current and the output/input resistance ratio
fields.example: β = 50, Ro = 5 kΩ, Ri = 1 kΩ. Find A_p?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting β is squared here, unlike voltage or current gain where it appears only once.
• Mixing up Ro(output resistance) and Ri (input resistance) in the ratio.
• Reporting Ap in dB without first converting properly (dB = 10log₁₀(Ap) for power ratios, not 20log₁₀).

fields.title: NAND / NOR Gates (Universal Gates)
fields.variables: Y = Evaluated output,  A,B = Logic gates,  NAND(NOT-AND),  NOR(NOT-OR)
fields.description: NAND is high when  atleast one input is low, NOR is high when both inputs are low.
fields.when_to_use: Used when designing discrete digital circuit arrays or simplifying boolean logic strings
fields.mnemonic:
“Universal = you can build anything from just one gate” — NAND and NOR alone can reconstruct
AND, OR, and NOT, which is why they're called universal gates.
fields.example: Build a NOT gate from a NAND gate: tie both inputs of the NAND together (A = B)
fields.answer: Y = NOT(A·A) = NOT(A) — a single NAND with shorted inputs behaves exactly like a NOT gate.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting NAND/NOR are “universal” precisely because NOT + AND/OR can each be built from
them alone.
• Mixing up De Morgan's equivalents: NOT(A·B) = Ā+B̄, not Ā·B̄.
• Assuming NAND and NOR give identical circuits for the same logic — they require different
wiring to build the same gate.

fields.title: Magnetic Field at Center of a Circular Loop
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field, μ₀ = Permittivity of free space, N =  Total turns,  I = Current, R = Coil radius
fields.description: Gives the magnetic field at the center of single circular current loop
fields.when_to_use: Used for specialised central baseline structural field magnitude evaluations where offsets steps x=0
fields.mnemonic: “The simplest loop formula” — turns × current, over twice the radius.
fields.example: N = 10 turns, I = 3 A, R = 0.05 m. Find B at the centre?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting to include N when it's a coil of multiple turns, not a single loop.
• Using the diameter instead of the radius R.
• Confusing this with the axial-field formula — this is just its special case at x = 0.

fields.title: Magnetic Field on Axis of a Circular Loop
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field, μ₀ = Permittivity of free space, I = Current, R = Ring radius, x = Distance from center axis node
fields.description: Gives magnetic field at any point on axis of circular loop
fields.when_to_use: Use to model field shapes anywhere along solitary circular conductive axis
fields.mnemonic: “Field fades fast off-axis — the 3/2 power is the giveaway that you're leaving the loop's plane.”
fields.example: I = 5 A, R = 0.05 m, x = 0.05 m. Find B on the axis?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Writing the power as 2 instead of 3/2 — the single most common slip in this formula.
• Forgetting to multiply by N if the coil has multiple turns.
• Not checking that at x = 0, this correctly reduces to the centre-of-loop formula B = μ0I/2R.

fields.title: Magnetic Field inside a Toroid
fields.variables: B = Magnetic field, μ₀ = Permittivity of free space, N = Total turns, I = Current, r = Average ring core radius
fields.description: Gives magnetic field confined within the core of toroidal coil
fields.when_to_use: Use when designing ring inductor cores or evaluating containment physics metrics
fields.mnemonic: “A toroid is a solenoid bent into a ring” — N turns wrapped around a circle of radius r
fields.example: N = 500 turns, I = 2 A, r = 0.1 m. Find B?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the field is zero both in the hollow centre of the toroid and outside it — it only
exists inside the windings.
• Using the tube's cross-sectional radius instead of r, the distance from the toroid's central axis
to the point.
• Forgetting N is the total number of turns, not turns per unit length.

fields.title: Force between two parallel current-carrying wires
fields.variables: F / L = Linear force density, μ₀ = Permittivity of free space, I1, I2 = Current,  d = Seperation between wires
fields.description: Two current-carrying wires attract if currents are parallel, and repels if anti-parallel
fields.when_to_use: Use to quantify static operational balance loads on parallel heavy transmissions line
fields.given_by: Ampère's Law (or the Biot-Savart law) and the Lorentz Force Law
fields.mnemonic: “Same-direction currents cuddle up (attract); opposite directions push apart.”
fields.example: I1= I2 = 5 A, d = 0.1 m. Find force per unit length?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Reporting F instead of F/L — the formula gives force per unit length, not total force.
• Forgetting the direction rule: parallel (same-direction) currents attract, antiparallel currents
repel.
• Mis-remembering μ0= 4π×10-7 T·m/A.

fields.title: Torque on a Current Loop/ Magnetic Diople
fields.variables: τ = Mechanical torque, m = Magnetic dipole moment, B = Magnetic field, θ = Normal angle
fields.description: Restoring torque experienced by a current loop or magnetic diople placed in an external field.
fields.when_to_use: Utilized inside electromechanical motor analysis or galvanometer loop calculations
fields.given_by: the fundamental magnetic force on a moving charge given by Lorentz force law
fields.mnemonic: “Edge-on to the field, maximum twist; face-on, no twist at all.”
fields.example: N = 50 turns, I = 2 A, area A = 0.01 m², B = 0.5 T, θ = 30° between m and B. Find torque?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting θ is measured between the magnetic moment (normal to the loop) and B — not
between the loop's plane and B.
• Skipping the step of computing m = NIA before using the torque formula.
• Forgetting torque is zero when the loop's plane is perpendicular to B (m parallel to B, θ = 0)

fields.title: Magnetic Moment of a Revolving Electron
fields.variables: μ = Magnetic dipole moment, L = Angular momentum, e = Charge of an electron, m_e = Mass of an electron
fields.description: Relates the angular momentum of an orbiting electron to its magnetic moment, from Bohr model.
fields.when_to_use: Use with atomic orbital physics computations to evaluate field interactions at sub-atomic scopes
fields.given_by: classical electromagnetism by treating the orbiting electron as a tiny current-carrying loop
fields.mnemonic:
“Half the charge-to-mass ratio, times angular momentum” — the orbital gyromagnetic ratio is
e/2m, not e/m.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator — a very common slip under exam pressure.
• Mixing this up with the electron's spin magnetic moment, which carries an extra g-factor (≈
2) and isn't simply e/2m.
• Using the wrong sign convention — for an electron, μL
 points opposite to L due to its negative
charge.

fields.title: Damped Oscillation Amplitude
fields.variables: A(t) = Peak amplitude at time t, A_0 = Initial amplitude limit, b = Damping force constant factor, m = Mass, t = Time
fields.description: Gives the exponential decay of oscillation amplitude caused by a resistive or damping force
fields.when_to_use: Use to calculate energy envelope collapse metrics inside dissipative medium systems
fields.given_by: the equation of motion (a second-order linear differential equation) using Newton's Second Law
fields.mnemonic: “Amplitude fades on an exponential curve — b is the brake, m is what resists it.”
fields.example:
A0
 = 0.1 m, b = 0.2 kg/s, m = 1 kg, t = 5 s. Find A(t)?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the factor of 2 in the denominator of the exponent.
• Confusing damping coefficient b with the spring constant k — they play very different roles.
• Assuming amplitude decays linearly with time; it's exponential, so it never quite reaches
zero.

fields.title: Time Period of a Physical Pendulum
fields.variables: T = Time period, I = Moment of inertia, m = Mass, g = Acceleration due to gravity, d = Distance
fields.description: Gives the period of rigid body oscillating about a fixed pivot under gravity.
fields.when_to_use: Use when dealing with real geometric distributions hanging from fixed pivot points
fields.given_by: the principles of rotational dynamics and Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
fields.mnemonic: “Same shape as the simple pendulum, but I replaces mL² and d replaces L.”
fields.example: I = 0.5 kg·m², m = 2 kg, g = 10 m/s², d = 0.3 m. Find T?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using the full length of the object instead of d, the distance from the pivot to the centre of
mass.
• Forgetting I must be the moment of inertia about the actual pivot axis (apply the parallel-axis
theorem if I is given about the centre of mass).
• Confusing this with the simple pendulum formula T = 2π√(L/g), which only applies to a point
mass on a string.

fields.title: Kinetic Energy in SHM
fields.variables: K = Kinetic energy, m = Mass, ω = Angular  frequency, A = Amplitude, x = Displacement
fields.description: Depicts the Kinetic energy of SHM in terms of angular frequency and amplitude of motion.
fields.when_to_use: Use to balance or find instant kinetic parameters across specific linear position frameworks
fields.given_by: the velocity of the oscillating particle as it moves through its path
fields.mnemonic: “KE is whatever total energy PE hasn't claimed yet — max at the centre.”
fields.example: m = 0.5 kg, ω = 4 rad/s, A = 0.1 m, x = 0.05 m. Find KE?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting KE + PE = ½mω²A² (constant total energy) — a good way to sanity-check answers.
• Swapping A and x by mistake, since both appear squared and look similar.
• Forgetting ω must be in rad/s, not frequency f (ω = 2πf).

fields.title: Potential Energy in SHM
fields.variables: U = Potential energy, m= Mass, ω= Angular frequency, x = Displacement from mean position
fields.description: Gives the energy possesed by a SHM at rest with angular frequency
fields.when_to_use: Use when isolating conservative structural harmonic grid molecules at a targeted spatial shift point
fields.given_by: The work done against conservative force to move an object/system into a new position
fields.mnemonic:
“PE grows like a bowl-shaped curve away from the centre — zero in the middle, max at the
ends.”
fields.example: m = 0.5 kg, ω = 4 rad/s, x = 0.05 m. Find PE ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting the ½ factor at the front.
• Using amplitude A instead of the instantaneous displacement x.
• Confusing this with total energy, which uses A² instead of x²: E = ½mω²A².

fields.title: Time Period of a Spring-Mass System
fields.variables: T = Time period, m = Initial mass load, k= Spring constant
fields.description: The period of oscillation of a mass attached to an ideal spring
fields.when_to_use: Use to discover cycle lengths or mass metrics for standard horizontal or vertical linear elastic spring setups
fields.given_by: Hooke's Law and Newton's Second Law for Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)
fields.mnemonic: “Heavier mass, lazier swing; stiffer spring, snappier swing”
fields.example: m = 2 kg, k = 200 N/m. Find T ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Assuming T depends on amplitude — it doesn't, SHM period is amplitude-independent.
• Using weight (mg) instead of mass (m) in the formula.
• Forgetting k must be in N/m and m in kg for the result to come out in seconds cleanly.

fields.title: Velocity in SHM
fields.variables: v = Instantaneous velocity, ω = Angular frequency, A = Amplitude, x = Displacement from mean position
fields.description: Gives speed of an SHM as function of its displacement
fields.when_to_use: Use to compute structural linear speed of any oscillating particle at given co-ordinate from its center point
fields.given_by: taking the time derivative of the displacement equation x(t)
fields.mnemonic: “Fastest at the centre, frozen at the edges” — v is max at x = 0, zero at x = ±A
fields.example: A = 0.1 m, ω = 10 rad/s, x = 0.06 m. Find v ?
fields.common_mistakes:
• Plugging in x > A, which is physically impossible and gives a negative number under the root.
• Confusing this with the acceleration formula a = −ω²x, which behaves oppositely (max at the
edges).
• Forgetting v is a speed here — direction depends on which way the object is moving.

fields.title: Reynolds Number
fields.variables: R_e = Reynolds number, ρ = Fluid density, v = Flow density, d = Pipe diameter, η = Dynamic viscosity
fields.description: Dimensionless number that predicts whether fluid flow will be laminar(Re < 2300)  or turbulent(Re > 4000)
fields.when_to_use: Use to mathematically classify whether a given fluid pipeline flow is laminar, transitional or turbulent
fields.mnemonic: “R_e tells you: calm river or rapids?” — it's inertial forces over viscous forces
fields.example:
ρ = 1000 kg/m³, v = 0.5 m/s, d = 0.02 m, η = 0.001 Pa·s.  Find R_e ?
.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing dynamic viscosity η with kinematic viscosity ν (= η/ρ) — they are not
interchangeable in the formula.
• Using the wrong “d” — it should be the characteristic length (pipe diameter, not radius).
• Forgetting flow is typically laminar below Re
 ≈ 2000 and turbulent above ≈ 4000 in pipes.

fields.title: Torricelli's Law
fields.variables: v = Velocity of efflux, g = Acceleration due to gravity, h = Depth of orifice below the open liquid surface
fields.description: Gives the speed at which liquid exits through a small hole below free surface of a container.
fields.when_to_use: Use to find exit speed of a liquid spilling out a small puncture or opening in open-top storage tank
fields.mnemonic: “Same speed as free-fall from height h” — Torricelli's law is just free fall in disguise
fields.example: Hole is h = 5 m below the water surface. Find efflux speed? (g = 10 m/s²)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Using the height of the tank instead of the height of liquid above the hole.
• Forgetting this assumes the tank is open to atmosphere and large compared to the hole.
• Applying it to viscous liquids, where real efflux speed is lower than predicted.

fields.title: Equation of Continuity
fields.variables: A1,A2 = Cross-sectional areas,  v1,v2 = Fluid velocities at these cross-sections
fields.description: Conservation of mass for incompresible, steady flow through a pipe of varying cross-section
fields.when_to_use: Use when an incompressible fluid moves through a pipe or channel of changing diameter to determine the velocity shift
fields.mnemonic: “Area shrinks, speed grows — flow rate stays true”
fields.example:
A1
 = 2 cm², v1
= 5 m/s, pipe narrows to A2
 = 1cm² Find v2
fields.common_mistakes:
• Assuming this holds for compressible flow (gases at high speed) — it's strictly for
incompressible fluids.
• Forgetting A depends on radius squared, so a small radius change causes a large area
change.
• Mixing units (cm² vs m²) between the two areas before comparing.

fields.title: Bernoulli's Equation
fields.variables: P = Static pressure, ρ = Fluid density, v = Fluid velocity, g = Acceleration due to gravity, h = Elevation height
fields.description: Conservation of energy along a streamline, relating pressure, speed and height in a flowing fluid
fields.when_to_use: Use when calculating fluid pressure, speed or height variations in a continuous, frictionless and incompressible streamline flow
fields.mnemonic: “Pressure + Speed² + Height — same total, everywhere along the flow”
fields.example:
Water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³): point 1, P1
 = 2×10^5
 Pa, v1= 2m/s, h1
= 0
. Point 2: h2
= 5 m, v2
= 4 m/s. Find P2
fields.common_mistakes:
• Applying it to a real (viscous) or compressible fluid, where it doesn't strictly hold.
• Picking two points that are not on the same streamline.
• Sign errors on height — always measure h from one consistent reference level.

fields.title: Angle of Deviation (Prism)
fields.variables: δ = Angle of deviation,  i1  = Angle of incidence,  i2  = Angle of emergence,   A = Prism (refracting) angle
fields.description: Gives the net angular deviation produced when a light ray passes through a prism, relating incidence, emergence, and prism angle
fields.when_to_use: When designing prisms for spectrometers or analyzing dispersion of light through optical wedges
fields.given_by: Isaac Newton in his 1666 prism experiments, which demonstrated that white light splits into its component colors — this formula, derived from Snell's Law applied at each refracting surface, quantifies exactly how much a ray bends after passing through a prism
fields.mnemonic:
“What goes in, minus what the prism keeps” — add both angles of incidence/emergence, then
subtract the prism's own angle.
fields.example:
At minimum deviation, i1
 = i2
 = 40°,  A = 60°.
fields.common_mistakes:
• Confusing A (the prism's refracting angle) with an angle of incidence.
• Forgetting that at minimum deviation, i1 = i2 and r1 = r2 = A/2.
• Applying the formula to a thin prism problem where the small-angle version δ = (n−1)A is
actually what's needed.

fields.title: Critical angle (Total internal reflection)
fields.variables: θ_c = Critical angle,  n = Refractive index of the denser medium relative to the rarer medium
fields.description: Gives the angle of incidence in a denser medium beyond which light is completely internally reflected at the boundary with a rarer medium
fields.when_to_use: When designing optical fibres, prisms, or analyzing mirage and total internal reflection phenomena
fields.given_by: the threshold angle beyond which light traveling from a denser to a rarer medium can no longer refract out — instead reflecting entirely back into the denser medium, the basis of total internal reflection
fields.mnemonic:
“Denser medium, smaller escape angle” — the higher the refractive index, the smaller θ
c
 becomes, so light escapes less easily
fields.worked_example: Glass-to-air interface, n = 1.5. Find the critical angle
fields.example: Glass-to-air interface, n = 1.5. Find the critical angle
fields.common_mistakes:
• Forgetting TIR only happens going from a denser to a rarer medium, never the reverse.
• Confusing the critical angle with Brewster's angle (tanθB
 = n) — different phenomenon
entirely.
• Using n as a ratio n2
/n1
 incorrectly when the light isn't going into vacuum/air

fields.title: Fringe width (Young's double slit)
fields.variables: β = Fringe width,   λ = Wavelength of light,  D = Distance from slits to screen,   d = Separation between the two slits
fields.description: Gives the spacing between consecutive bright or dark fringes produced by two coherent interfering light sources
fields.when_to_use: When analyzing interference patterns in double-slit experiments or designing interferometers
fields.mnemonic:
fringes spread out with screen distance (D) and squeeze
 together with slit gap (d)
fields.example: λ = 500 nm, D = 1 m, d = 1 mm. Find fringe width
fields.common_mistakes:
• Swapping D (slit-to-screen distance) and d (slit separation) — they look similar but are very
different scales.
• Forgetting the position of the n-th bright fringe is y = nβ, not β itself.
• Leaving λ in nm while D, d are in m — always convert to one consistent unit first

fields.title: Single Slit Diffraction (Minima Condition)
fields.variables: a = Slit width,  θ = Angle of diffraction,  n = Order of minimum (integer),   λ = Wavelength of light
fields.description: Gives the angular positions of dark fringes (minima) produced when light diffracts through a narrow single slit
fields.when_to_use: When predicting the diffraction pattern width for slits, apertures, or spectrometer design
fields.given_by: Derived from Huygens' Principle treating the slit as interfering wavelets; note this gives minima, not maxima
fields.mnemonic:
“Minima means integer” — the dark fringes of a single slit use whole numbers (n = 1, 2, 3…),
the opposite of YDSE where whole numbers give bright fringes
fields.example:
Given slit width a = 0.2 mm, light of λ = 600 nm. 
Find the angle of the first minimum (n = 1)
fields.common_mistakes:
• Mixing this up with YDSE, where nλ gives bright fringes, not dark ones

• Forgetting n = 0 is the central maximum, not a minimum — the formula starts from n = 1

• Not converting a and λ to the same unit before dividing
